guides.title: Soil Testing and Interpreting the Results
guides.summary: A complete guide to sampling soil, reading a laboratory report, and turning the numbers into decisions, covering pH, cation exchange, macro- and micronutrients, organic matter, texture, salinity and contaminants. It explains the mechanisms behind each measurement, the arithmetic of unit conversion and amendment rates, and how to diagnose results that contradict what the field is doing.

sections.heading: Why Soil Is Tested at All
sections.body:
Every decision a grower makes about fertiliser, lime, compost or irrigation is a bet about what is
already in the ground. Soil testing converts that bet into a measurement. Without it, the usual
practice is to fertilise by habit, by the recommendation printed on a bag, or by the appearance of
the crop, and all three are unreliable. A yellowing leaf can mean nitrogen shortage, but it can just
as easily mean waterlogged roots, sulphur deficiency, iron unavailable because the soil is too
alkaline, or root damage from nematodes. Applying nitrogen to a soil that is short of sulphur wastes
money and can make the imbalance worse. A test replaces guesswork with numbers, and numbers can be
compared across seasons.

The economic case is straightforward. A standard agronomic test in most countries costs roughly the
equivalent of one to two bags of compound fertiliser, and it is usually good for two to four years
on a stable field because pH and phosphorus move slowly. Against that, over-application is expensive
and often invisible: excess phosphorus does not usually scorch a crop, it simply sits there,
unavailable to the plant and available to the next heavy rain, which carries it into waterways where
it drives algal blooms. Under-application is equally invisible until harvest, by which time it cannot
be corrected. The test is the only cheap way to see which of the two mistakes is being made.

There is a second, quieter reason. Soil chemistry is not intuitive, and the plant's response to a
nutrient is rarely proportional to how much is added. The classic description is Liebig's law of the
minimum, articulated in the 1840s by the German chemist Justus von Liebig: growth is limited by the
scarcest necessary resource, not by the total supply of all of them. Adding more of something already
sufficient produces no response. This is why growers so often report that a fertiliser "stopped
working" after a few good years. It did not stop working; the limiting factor moved to something
else, and only a test reveals where it moved to.

Testing also protects against harm that has nothing to do with yield. Urban and peri-urban soils
routinely carry lead from pre-1980 paint and leaded petrol, and a vegetable bed on the drip line of
an old house can measure several hundred parts per million of lead where the surrounding lawn
measures thirty. No visual inspection detects this. Neither does taste, smell, or plant vigour, since
most vegetables tolerate lead levels that are unsafe for the people eating them. In that setting a
one-off heavy-metal screen is not an agronomic refinement; it is a basic safety measure, and it is
the single most valuable test an urban grower can buy.

sections.heading: What Soil Is Made Of
sections.body:
A productive mineral topsoil is, by volume, roughly forty-five percent mineral particles, five
percent organic matter, and fifty percent pore space, with that pore space split about evenly
between water and air when the soil is at field capacity. Those proportions matter more than any
single nutrient number, because they determine whether roots can breathe, whether water infiltrates
or runs off, and whether the chemistry a laboratory measures is actually reachable by a root.

The mineral fraction is classified by particle size, and the boundaries are conventional but
internationally fairly consistent. Sand runs from 0.05 to 2 millimetres in the USDA system, silt from
0.002 to 0.05 millimetres, and clay is everything finer than 0.002 millimetres. Anything larger than
2 millimetres is gravel and is excluded from the texture calculation entirely, which is why a stony
field can test as a loam while behaving in practice like a sieve. The size difference is not merely
descriptive: it drives surface area. A gram of coarse sand offers something on the order of 0.01
square metres of surface, a gram of silt perhaps 0.5, and a gram of montmorillonite clay can offer
600 to 800 square metres. Nearly all of soil chemistry, the holding of nutrients and water alike,
happens on those surfaces, which is why clay content dominates a soil's chemical behaviour out of all
proportion to its weight.

Organic matter is the partly decomposed residue of everything that has lived in and on the soil. It
is conventionally about fifty-eight percent carbon, which is why laboratories that burn a sample to
measure carbon multiply the result by 1.72 to report organic matter. Its influence is
disproportionate: humified organic matter has a nutrient-holding capacity several times that of the
best clay, holds several times its own weight in water, glues mineral particles into crumbs, and
slowly releases nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur as microbes consume it. A one percentage point rise
in organic matter in the top 15 centimetres of a hectare represents very roughly twenty tonnes of
added material, which is why building it is measured in decades, not seasons.

The living fraction is small by mass, typically well under one percent, and enormous by influence. A
gram of healthy topsoil holds on the order of a billion bacteria across tens of thousands of species,
several hundred metres of fungal hyphae, and a population of protozoa, nematodes, mites and
earthworms that cycle nutrients by eating each other. Most nitrogen a plant takes up has passed
through a microbe first. The pore space they occupy is created and maintained by roots, worms and
fungal threads, which is the mechanism by which biology feeds back into physics.

sections.heading: Soil pH: The Master Variable
sections.body:
If only one number could be measured, it should be pH. It is a logarithmic measure of hydrogen ion
activity in the soil solution, running in practice from about 3.5 in acid peat to about 10 in a
sodic desert soil, with most agricultural soils falling between 5.0 and 8.5. Because the scale is
logarithmic, a soil at pH 5.0 is ten times more acidic than one at 6.0 and a hundred times more
acidic than one at 7.0. This is the single most misread fact on a soil report: the difference between
5.5 and 6.5 is not a small adjustment, it is an order of magnitude.

The reason pH dominates is that it governs the solubility, and therefore the availability, of nearly
every nutrient. Phosphorus is the clearest case. Below about pH 5.5 it precipitates with iron and
aluminium into compounds a root cannot dissolve; above about pH 7.5 it precipitates with calcium as
various calcium phosphates. Its availability peaks in a fairly narrow window around 6.0 to 7.0. This
means a soil can hold plenty of total phosphorus and starve the crop of it, and adding more
phosphate fertiliser to an acid soil largely feeds the same precipitation reaction. Correcting the pH
releases what is already there and is usually the cheaper intervention.

The micronutrients run the other way. Iron, manganese, zinc, copper and boron all become more soluble
as pH falls. Below about 5.2, aluminium and manganese can reach concentrations that are directly
toxic to roots, stunting them into short, thickened stubs that cannot explore for water. Aluminium
toxicity, not acidity as such, is what actually kills crops on strongly acid soils. Above about 7.5,
iron and manganese become so insoluble that susceptible plants such as blueberries, azaleas and some
citrus show interveinal chlorosis, yellow leaves with green veins, even though the soil contains
abundant iron.

Biology tracks pH too. The bacteria that convert ammonium to nitrate work best between about 6.0 and
8.0 and slow markedly below 5.5, so acid soils accumulate ammonium and mineralise nitrogen sluggishly.
Rhizobium bacteria that fix nitrogen in legume nodules are similarly sensitive, which is why lucerne
and clover fail on acid ground while the grass beside them survives. Earthworm populations thin below
about pH 4.5.

Reports may quote two different pH numbers and confusing them causes real errors. Water pH is measured
in a slurry of soil and distilled water and is the number most people mean. Buffer pH, sometimes
called lime requirement index, is measured after adding a buffering solution and does not describe the
soil's acidity at all; it measures reserve acidity held on exchange sites, and it is the number that
determines how much lime is actually needed.

sections.heading: Cation Exchange Capacity and Base Saturation
sections.body:
Clay particles and humified organic matter carry a permanent net negative electrical charge on their
surfaces. Because most plant nutrients dissolve as positively charged ions, or cations, those negative
surfaces act as a rechargeable store, holding calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium, ammonium,
hydrogen and aluminium loosely enough that roots can pull them off but tightly enough that rain
cannot wash them away. The total size of that store is the cation exchange capacity, universally
abbreviated CEC, and it is the single best one-number description of how a soil will behave.

CEC is reported in centimoles of charge per kilogram, written cmol(+)/kg, which is numerically
identical to the older unit milliequivalents per hundred grams, meq/100g. Seeing both on the same
report does not mean two different measurements; the numbers are the same. Typical values run from 1
to 5 in a coarse sand, 5 to 15 in a sandy loam, 15 to 30 in a silt loam or clay loam, and 30 to 60 in
a heavy clay or a peat. Organic matter contributes roughly 2 to 3 cmol(+)/kg for every one percent
of organic matter, so raising organic matter from 2 to 4 percent on a sandy soil can lift its CEC by
half again, which is a real and durable improvement.

The practical consequences are immediate. A sand with a CEC of 3 has almost no capacity to hold
potassium or ammonium against leaching, so on such a soil the correct strategy is small, frequent
applications rather than one large one, and a single heavy dose of soluble potassium may largely be
gone after 50 millimetres of rain. A clay with a CEC of 35 holds a large reserve, responds slowly to
amendment, and requires far more lime to shift its pH because most of its acidity is held on exchange
sites rather than dissolved in solution. This is precisely why buffer pH exists as a separate
measurement.

Base saturation is the percentage of that exchange capacity occupied by the so-called basic cations,
calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium, with the remainder held by hydrogen and aluminium. It
correlates tightly with pH: a soil at 80 percent base saturation is usually near neutral, one at 40
percent is usually strongly acid. Reports often break the figure down by element, giving something
like 65 percent calcium, 12 percent magnesium, 4 percent potassium.

Here honesty is required, because this is genuinely contested ground. One school, the basic cation
saturation ratio approach originating with Bear and later popularised by Albrecht, holds that there is
an ideal ratio, commonly cited as about 65 percent calcium, 10 percent magnesium and 5 percent
potassium, and that yield suffers when soils depart from it. Decades of replicated field trials,
including the widely cited Wisconsin work of McLean and colleagues, have largely failed to
demonstrate yield responses to correcting ratios once each nutrient is individually sufficient. The
mainstream agronomic position is that sufficiency levels matter and ratios mostly do not, within
broad limits. Extremes still matter: magnesium above roughly 25 percent of CEC degrades soil
structure, and sodium above 15 percent causes clay dispersion.

sections.heading: Nitrogen, Phosphorus and Potassium
sections.body:
The three nutrients printed on every fertiliser bag are the ones crops need in the largest amounts,
and each behaves so differently in soil that they require different testing logic entirely.

Nitrogen is the awkward one, and the most common reason a soil test disappoints. The great majority
of soil nitrogen, typically 95 percent or more, is locked in organic matter and unavailable until
microbes mineralise it into ammonium and then nitrate. Mineralisation rate depends on temperature,
moisture and the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of the residue, so it changes week by week. Nitrate carries
a negative charge, is therefore repelled rather than held by exchange sites, and leaches with the
first heavy rain. A nitrate measurement is consequently a snapshot with a short shelf life, and many
laboratories in humid regions decline to offer it for that reason, estimating nitrogen supply from
organic matter content and cropping history instead. Where nitrate testing is genuinely useful is in
dry climates, where the pre-plant deep nitrate test, sampling to 60 or 90 centimetres, reliably finds
carryover nitrogen. A useful rule of thumb is that each one percent of organic matter mineralises
roughly 10 to 20 kilograms of nitrogen per hectare per season in a temperate climate, more in a warm
one.

Phosphorus is the opposite: almost immobile, and therefore very well suited to testing. It moves
perhaps a centimetre or two a year by diffusion, so a measurement stays valid for several seasons.
The catch is that no extraction measures total phosphorus usefully, because most of it is chemically
locked. Laboratories instead use an extractant chosen to mimic what a root can access, and the
choice depends on soil pH. Bray-1, a dilute acid fluoride, is standard for acid to neutral soils but
is destroyed by free carbonate, so it gives falsely low readings on calcareous ground. Olsen, a
sodium bicarbonate extraction at pH 8.5, is the standard for calcareous soils. Mehlich-3 is a
multi-element extractant now widely used across a broad pH range. The numbers are not interchangeable:
an Olsen value of 15 mg/kg and a Bray value of 15 mg/kg describe quite different soils.

Potassium sits in between. It is a cation, so it is held on exchange sites and measured reliably by
the same ammonium acetate or Mehlich extraction used for calcium and magnesium. It leaches
appreciably only on sandy, low-CEC soils. Its complication is fixation: certain clay minerals,
particularly illite and vermiculite, trap potassium between their layers when the soil dries and
release it when it wets, so readings can swing seasonally on the same field. Interpretation must
therefore be tied to CEC. A potassium reading of 120 mg/kg is comfortable on a sand with a CEC of 5
and marginal on a clay with a CEC of 30, because the clay's larger reserve dilutes the same quantity
across far more exchange sites.

sections.heading: Secondary Nutrients and Micronutrients
sections.body:
Beyond the familiar three, plants require calcium, magnesium and sulphur in appreciable quantities
and a further set of elements in trace amounts. Deficiency in any of them caps yield exactly as
firmly as a shortage of nitrogen, and because they are rarely applied routinely, they are a common
hidden constraint on long-cropped ground.

Calcium and magnesium are usually reported alongside potassium as exchangeable cations. Calcium
deficiency in the strict sense is rare in soils above pH 6, because liming supplies it in bulk;
what looks like calcium deficiency in the field, such as blossom-end rot in tomatoes or bitter pit in
apples, is nearly always a transport problem caused by irregular watering rather than a soil
shortage, since calcium moves only in the transpiration stream and cannot be redistributed once
deposited. Magnesium deficiency is genuinely common on sandy acid soils and on ground limed
repeatedly with pure calcitic limestone, which supplies calcium while the crop removes magnesium.
Dolomitic limestone, which contains both, is the standard correction, and interveinal yellowing of
older leaves is the classic symptom.

Sulphur has become far more important than it was. Historically, industrial emissions deposited
substantial sulphur from the atmosphere, in some industrial regions 20 to 40 kilograms per hectare
per year. Clean-air legislation from the 1970s onward cut that dramatically, and sulphur deficiency
has emerged accordingly, particularly in oilseeds and brassicas, which have high requirements.
Sulphate behaves chemically much like nitrate, carrying a negative charge and leaching readily, so
soil tests for it are only moderately reliable and many advisers prefer plant tissue analysis.

Among the micronutrients, zinc, boron, iron, manganese, copper, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel are
the eight generally recognised as essential. The quantities involved are tiny: a maize crop might
remove 300 grams of zinc per hectare against 150 kilograms of nitrogen. Zinc deficiency is the most
widespread globally, common on high-pH, high-phosphorus and eroded soils, and it has genuine human
consequences because zinc-poor grain produces zinc-poor diets. Boron deficiency affects brassicas,
beet and many fruit crops, showing as hollow or corky stem and root tissue.

Boron deserves a specific warning. The margin between deficiency and toxicity is narrower than for
any other nutrient, often only a factor of two or three in soil concentration. Deficiency may appear
below about 0.5 mg/kg of hot-water-extractable boron and toxicity above roughly 2 to 4 mg/kg
depending on species. Correction rates are typically 1 to 2 kilograms of actual boron per hectare,
and applying a garden-scale equivalent by eye, or broadcasting it unevenly, has poisoned more crops
than it has rescued. Boron should be applied only on a test result, dissolved and sprayed for
evenness, and never guessed.

sections.heading: Organic Matter, Carbon and Biological Measures
sections.body:
Organic matter appears on almost every soil report as a single percentage, and that percentage
carries more information about a soil's long-run behaviour than any nutrient figure. It is normally
determined by loss on ignition, in which a dried sample is weighed, heated to around 360 to 550
degrees Celsius until the organic fraction burns away, and weighed again, the mass loss being taken
as organic matter. The alternative is the Walkley-Black wet oxidation with dichromate, which measures
organic carbon and is then multiplied by the conventional factor of 1.72. Neither is perfect. Loss on
ignition also drives off structural water from clay minerals and can decompose carbonates at the
upper end of that temperature range, so it tends to overstate organic matter on heavy clay and
calcareous soils. Walkley-Black typically recovers only about 75 to 80 percent of the carbon present
and applies a correction factor to compensate. Comparing an ignition result from one laboratory to a
Walkley-Black result from another is therefore not a like-for-like comparison, and a year-on-year
trend is only meaningful if the method has stayed the same.

Typical values are worth memorising as a frame of reference. A degraded, long-tilled arable sand may
run 0.8 to 1.5 percent, a well-managed arable loam 2 to 4 percent, permanent pasture 4 to 8 percent,
a woodland topsoil 6 to 12 percent, and a drained peat 20 percent and upward. Movement is slow and
that slowness is the honest headline: under continuous good management, a realistic gain is on the
order of 0.1 percentage points a year, and it plateaus. Claims of doubling organic matter in three
seasons should be treated with scepticism unless very large quantities of imported material were
applied, in which case what was measured is the material itself, not stabilised humus.

The measurement's weakness is that it lumps together fractions with wildly different behaviour. Fresh
crop residue, actively decomposing particulate material and centuries-old mineral-bound humus all
count identically, yet only the active fraction supplies nutrients this season while only the stable
fraction confers durable structure. Some laboratories now separate these, offering particulate
organic matter, permanganate-oxidisable or active carbon, or a 24-hour carbon dioxide burst that
measures how much the soil respires when rewetted. These give a more responsive signal of biological
condition, changing within a season or two rather than a decade.

Formal biological tests exist but should be bought with clear eyes. Microbial biomass carbon,
enzyme assays such as beta-glucosidase, phospholipid fatty acid profiling and DNA sequencing of the
microbial community are all real measurements. What is largely missing is a validated translation
from any of those numbers into a management decision or a fertiliser rate. They describe condition;
they do not yet reliably prescribe action. The cheapest useful biological indicators remain visual
and free: earthworm counts in a 20-centimetre spade cube, the smell of the soil, how readily a moist
clod crumbles along natural fracture planes, and how fast water disappears from a ring pressed into
the surface.

sections.heading: Texture, Structure and the Physical Tests
sections.body:
Chemistry describes what is present; physics decides whether a root can reach it. A soil with textbook
nutrient levels and a compacted plough pan at 20 centimetres will underperform a chemically mediocre
soil that roots can occupy freely, and no laboratory report will show it. The physical assessment is
made in the field, largely with a spade, and it is the half of soil testing most often skipped.

Texture, the proportion of sand, silt and clay, is measured in the laboratory by particle-size
analysis, usually the hydrometer or pipette method, in which the sample is dispersed with a chemical
such as sodium hexametaphosphate and the settling rate is timed. Stokes' law governs the process:
larger particles fall faster, so sand settles within about 40 seconds, silt over several hours, and
clay remains suspended for a day or more. The proportions are plotted on the standard textural
triangle to yield a class name such as sandy clay loam. Texture is effectively permanent. It cannot
be changed by any practical amendment at field scale, a point worth being blunt about, since adding
sand to clay in less than overwhelming quantities produces something closer to concrete than to loam.

A serviceable field estimate needs only water and hands. Moisten a walnut-sized lump to the
consistency of putty and knead it until it is uniform. If it will not form a ball at all, it is sand.
If it forms a ball that crumbles when pressed, loamy sand. Roll it into a cylinder about the thickness
of a pencil: if it holds, there is meaningful clay. Bend that cylinder into a ring; if it forms
without cracking, clay content is likely above about 35 percent. Silt announces itself as a smooth,
soapy or floury feel, clay as sticky and plastic, sand as audibly gritty when worked near the ear.
With practice this places a soil within one class of laboratory analysis.

Structure, unlike texture, is entirely manageable and matters more day to day. It describes how
particles aggregate into crumbs, blocks or plates. Dig a pit to at least 40 centimetres, ideally with
one vertical face, and read it. Good structure shows rounded crumbs a few millimetres to a centimetre
across, abundant visible pores, roots running in all directions, and clods that fracture into smaller
crumbs when dropped. Damaged structure shows horizontal plates, sharp-edged massive clods, roots
turning sideways at a definite depth, and grey or blue-grey mottling that indicates prolonged
waterlogging and oxygen starvation.

Two quick quantitative tests are worth the time. Infiltration is measured by driving an open pipe of
about 15 centimetres diameter a few centimetres into the surface, adding 25 millimetres of water, and
timing its disappearance; under a minute suggests a coarse or cracked soil, one to ten minutes is
generally healthy, and beyond thirty minutes indicates a serious sealing or compaction problem. Slake
testing, dropping an air-dried aggregate into a jar of clean water, shows aggregate stability: a
well-aggregated crumb holds together for minutes, while a degraded one collapses into a cloud within
seconds.

sections.heading: Taking a Sample That Actually Represents the Field
sections.body:
The laboratory analyses perhaps ten grams of soil and reports a number for a field of ten thousand
tonnes. Sampling error is routinely larger than analytical error by an order of magnitude, and it is
entirely under the control of the person holding the spade. The core principle is to define a
management unit that is genuinely uniform and to composite many small cores from within it. Twelve to
twenty cores bulked into one sample is the standard minimum for a uniform area up to about two
hectares. Ground that differs visibly in colour, drainage, slope or cropping history must be sampled
separately, because averaging a wet hollow with a dry knoll produces a number describing neither.

Depth must match the question and stay constant between years. Arable and vegetable ground is
conventionally sampled 0 to 15 or 0 to 20 centimetres, matching the cultivated layer. Permanent
pasture and no-till use 0 to 10 centimetres, because immobile nutrients and lime stratify sharply at
the surface where they are applied and a deeper core dilutes them. Sampling to an inconsistent depth
is the commonest way to manufacture a spurious trend across years.
ingredients: A soil auger, stainless steel probe or clean spade; avoid galvanised or brass tools when zinc or copper are being tested, as they contaminate the sample
A clean plastic bucket for compositing, again not galvanised
Sample bags from the laboratory, or clean bags of about half a litre
A permanent marker, and a notebook or phone for positions and field history
steps: Divide the property into management units of uniform soil type, slope, drainage and cropping history. Sketch them on a map and give each a permanent name you will reuse in future years.
Deliberately exclude atypical spots: gateways, stock camps, troughs, old manure or burn sites, fence lines, headlands and anywhere fertiliser has spilled.
Walk each unit in a zigzag or W pattern so cores spread across the whole area rather than clustering along one edge.

At each stop, scrape aside surface litter, then take a core of uniform diameter to the chosen depth. With a spade, cut a V-shaped hole, slice a 2-centimetre vertical wafer from one face, and trim it to a central strip of even width.
Drop every core into the same bucket: 15 to 20 for a uniform unit, more if the ground is variable.
Mix the bucket thoroughly by hand until the composite looks uniform, removing stones, roots and surface residue.
Fill one bag with about 500 grams of the mix. Label it immediately with unit name, depth and date, on the bag itself rather than only on a tag.
If nitrate is measured, keep the sample cool and deliver it within 24 hours, or air-dry it thinly in shade, because microbes keep converting nitrogen in a warm moist bag.
Record crop, previous crop, yield and two years of fertiliser, lime and manure applications on the submission form; without that history no sensible recommendation is possible.
Sample at the same point in the year each cycle, ideally after harvest and before amendment, so results stay comparable.

sections.heading: Extraction Chemistry and Why Laboratories Disagree
sections.body:
A recurring and genuinely bewildering experience is sending split samples of the same soil to two
laboratories and receiving phosphorus values that differ by a factor of three. Neither laboratory is
necessarily wrong. They measured different things and both reported the answer to their own question.

The root of it is that there is no such thing as a plant-available nutrient pool with sharp
boundaries. Nutrients exist along a continuum from fully dissolved in soil water, through loosely
adsorbed on mineral surfaces, to firmly bound in compounds that release over decades, to locked in
primary minerals. A root accesses part of that continuum, and the fraction it can reach depends on
the crop, the season and the root architecture. A chemical extractant is a deliberate simplification:
a solution chosen because, empirically, the quantity it dissolves correlates with crop response in
field trials. It is a proxy calibrated against yield, not a measurement of a physically real
quantity.

Different regions built different proxies, and each is calibrated to its own soils. Mehlich-3, a
dilute mixture of acetic and nitric acids with ammonium fluoride and EDTA, extracts phosphorus,
potassium, calcium, magnesium and several micronutrients in one operation and is now dominant across
much of North America. Bray-1 uses hydrochloric acid and ammonium fluoride and works well on acid to
neutral soils but is neutralised by carbonate, so it under-reports badly above about pH 7.2. Olsen's
sodium bicarbonate at pH 8.5 was designed for calcareous soils. Ammonium acetate at pH 7 is the
classical exchangeable-cation extractant. Morgan and modified Morgan, weak acetate solutions, are
used in parts of the northeastern United States and give characteristically low numbers. In much of
Europe, calcium chloride, calcium acetate lactate or ammonium lactate methods prevail.

The consequence is that an interpretation category, low, medium, optimum, high, only means something
in the context of the specific method and its local calibration. A Morgan phosphorus of 8 mg/kg may be
classed optimum where a Mehlich-3 value of 8 would be classed very low. Rough conversion equations
between methods exist in the literature, but their scatter is wide enough that they should be treated
as indicative only, never used to replace a proper test.

Three practical rules follow. First, choose one laboratory and stay with it, because trends over time
are only interpretable within a consistent method. Second, always read the units and the method name
printed on the report before reacting to any number, and if the method is not stated, ask. Third,
trust the interpretation category over the raw number, because the category encodes the laboratory's
local calibration against actual yield trials, which is knowledge you do not otherwise have access
to. If a laboratory reports a number without a category or a recommendation, and cannot say what
crop response its calibration was built from, that report is much less useful than its precision
implies.

sections.heading: Home Kits, Meters and Field Tests
sections.body:
The gap between a laboratory analysis and a hardware-store kit is wide, and understanding exactly
where each fails prevents both misplaced trust and unnecessary dismissal.

Colorimetric kits, the familiar tubes in which soil is shaken with an extracting powder and the
resulting colour compared against a printed chart, use chemistry that is real. Phosphorus is
determined by molybdenum blue, nitrate by a reduction and diazotisation reaction, potassium by
turbidimetry with sodium tetraphenylborate. Their weaknesses are practical rather than theoretical.
The extractants are weak and generic, so results are not calibrated to any particular soil type.
Reading a colour by eye under varying light is imprecise, particularly for the roughly eight percent
of men with some form of colour vision deficiency. Reagents degrade, and a kit more than two or three
years old, or one stored somewhere hot, will read low. In practice these kits distinguish very low
from very high with fair reliability and cannot resolve the medium range where nearly all real
decisions are made.

The pH testing in such kits is more trustworthy than the nutrient tests, because pH indicator dyes
are robust and the colour change is large. A careful indicator test gives pH to about half a unit,
which is genuinely useful for deciding whether to lime at all, though not for calculating how much.

The cheap two-prong or three-prong meters sold as pH-and-moisture testers deserve blunt treatment.
The ones with no battery work by galvanic action between two dissimilar metals inserted into moist
soil. They respond primarily to soil moisture and to dissolved salts, and their pH scale is very
loosely related to actual acidity. In side-by-side comparisons they frequently read near seven in
soils that measure four or nine. They should not be used for any decision. A genuine electronic pH
meter with a glass electrode, calibrated before each use against buffer solutions at pH 4.0 and 7.0
and used in a properly prepared soil-water slurry, is accurate to about 0.1 units and is a legitimate
instrument, but it costs many times more, needs its electrode kept wet in storage solution, and needs
recalibrating regularly.

Two free field tests deserve their reputation. The vinegar and baking soda test detects extremes: a
teaspoon of soil that fizzes with vinegar contains free carbonate and is certainly alkaline, above
about pH 7.5, while a moist sample that fizzes with baking soda is strongly acid, below about pH 5.
No reaction from either simply means the soil is somewhere in the middle, which covers most soils and
tells you little. The jar or Mason-jar sedimentation test, in which soil is shaken with water and a
pinch of dispersant and left to settle in layers, gives a rough texture reading in a day. Both are
crude, both are honest about being crude, and both are more useful than a device that returns a
precise-looking number derived from nothing.

sections.heading: Reading the Report: Units and Arithmetic
sections.body:
Soil reports are dense with numbers in inconsistent units, and unit confusion is a leading cause of
serious over-application. Working through the arithmetic once makes every subsequent report legible.

The most common concentration unit is milligrams per kilogram, mg/kg, which is numerically identical
to parts per million, ppm. If a report gives one and a neighbouring column gives the other, they are
the same measurement. Many North American reports instead give pounds per acre, and the conversion
rests on a convention: an acre of soil to a depth of about 17 centimetres, roughly six and two-thirds
inches, is taken to weigh two million pounds. Therefore pounds per acre equals ppm multiplied by two.
A soil at 30 ppm phosphorus is reported as 60 pounds per acre. Reading 60 as though it were a
concentration doubles your apparent fertility and can lead to skipping an application that was
needed. The metric equivalent uses a hectare of soil 15 centimetres deep at a bulk density of 1.3,
which weighs about 2 million kilograms, so kilograms per hectare is roughly ppm multiplied by two as
well, a coincidence that is convenient but should still be checked against the report's own footnote.

Phosphorus and potassium carry a second trap inherited from the fertiliser trade. Fertiliser analysis
is quoted as nitrogen, then phosphorus as phosphorus pentoxide, P2O5, then potassium as potassium
oxide, K2O. Neither oxide exists in the bag; the convention is a nineteenth-century relic. Soil
reports may use either the elemental or the oxide basis. To convert elemental phosphorus to P2O5,
multiply by 2.29; to go the other way, multiply by 0.436. For potassium to K2O, multiply by 1.2; the
reverse is 0.83. A bag marked 10-20-10 supplies 20 percent P2O5, which is only 8.7 percent actual
phosphorus. Mixing the two bases has produced application errors of well over a factor of two.

Cation figures may be given in mg/kg or in cmol(+)/kg, and converting requires dividing by the
equivalent weight, which is the atomic mass divided by the charge. For calcium, atomic mass 40 and
charge 2, the equivalent weight is 20, so 2000 mg/kg of calcium is 2000 divided by 20 divided by 10,
giving 10 cmol(+)/kg. For magnesium the divisor is 12.15, for potassium 39.1, for sodium 23. The
extra division by ten converts from milligrams per kilogram to centimoles per kilogram.

One worked example ties it together. A report reads: pH 5.8, organic matter 3.1 percent, Mehlich-3
phosphorus 12 mg/kg, potassium 95 mg/kg, calcium 1100 mg/kg, magnesium 130 mg/kg, CEC 11
cmol(+)/kg. Potassium as a fraction of CEC is 95 divided by 39.1 divided by 10, giving 0.243
cmol(+)/kg, which is 2.2 percent of CEC, at the low end. Calcium is 1100 over 20 over 10, giving 5.5,
or exactly half of CEC, which is modest and consistent with the mildly acid pH.

sections.heading: Sufficiency Versus Build-and-Maintain
sections.body:
Two soil test reports on identical soil can yield fertiliser recommendations that differ threefold,
not because the chemistry is disputed but because the two laboratories follow different philosophies
about what a soil test is for. Knowing which philosophy is being applied is essential to reading any
recommendation intelligently.

The sufficiency level approach asks a single question: will adding this nutrient, this season, pay
for itself? It rests on the yield response curve described by Mitscherlich in 1909, in which each
additional increment of a nutrient produces a smaller yield gain than the last, approaching a plateau
asymptotically. Below a critical level, usually defined as the concentration at which a crop achieves
about 95 percent of its maximum yield, application pays handsomely. Above it, response is negligible
and money is wasted. A sufficiency programme therefore fertilises heavily on deficient soils, lightly
on marginal ones, and not at all above the critical level, allowing soil test values to drift
downward on rich ground until they approach that threshold. It maximises return per unit of
fertiliser and minimises environmental loss. Its cost is risk: soil values sit close to the critical
line, so a sampling error, an unusually good season or a missed application can cause a real yield
penalty with no reserve to buffer it.

The build-and-maintain approach asks a different question: what soil test value do I want this field
to hold indefinitely? It applies enough to raise a deficient soil to a chosen target over several
years, the build phase, then applies roughly what the crop removes each year, the maintenance phase.
Removal figures are well documented; maize grain removes roughly 3.4 kilograms of P2O5 and 3.0 of K2O
per tonne, wheat grain about 4 and 3, and a hay crop far more potassium because the whole plant
leaves the field. This approach buys insurance. It is more forgiving of sampling error and poor
timing, spreads cash flow smoothly, and suits rented ground poorly but owned ground well. Its cost is
capital tied up in soil reserves that may never be needed, and a higher risk of phosphorus loss to
water from soils held above agronomic requirement.

Neither is wrong. Which is right depends on circumstances that no laboratory can know: the price
ratio between fertiliser and crop, whether the land is owned or rented, the grower's tolerance for
risk, distance to sensitive water, and the soil's fixation capacity. On a highly phosphorus-fixing
tropical soil, building a reserve can be prohibitively expensive because much of what is applied is
locked away, and sufficiency is generally the rational choice. On a well-buffered temperate loam
farmed long-term, building has a strong case.

The honest warning is about a third pattern, in which a recommendation arrives from a supplier who
also sells the products. This is not automatically corrupt, and many such advisers are excellent, but
the incentive runs one direction. The check is to ask which philosophy the recommendation follows,
what critical level it uses, and what field trial data supports that level for your crop and region.
A confident adviser will answer readily.

sections.heading: From Report to Amendment: The Calculations
sections.body:
The point of a report is a decision, and turning one into the other requires arithmetic that is not
difficult but is unforgiving of carelessness. Two calculations cover the great majority of cases:
how much lime, and how much of a given fertiliser.

Lime first, because pH correction should almost always precede nutrient correction. Adding phosphorus
to a soil at pH 5.2 partly wastes it to iron and aluminium fixation, whereas liming first releases
phosphorus already present. The quantity required is not derived from water pH but from buffer pH or
an equivalent exchangeable acidity measurement, because it is reserve acidity on exchange sites, not
the small quantity dissolved in solution, that must be neutralised. As a rough order of magnitude, a
sandy soil may need 1 to 2 tonnes of ground limestone per hectare to raise pH one unit, a loam 3 to 5
tonnes, and a heavy clay or high organic matter soil 6 to 10 tonnes. Applying a clay rate to a sand
will overshoot into alkalinity and induce micronutrient deficiencies that take years to correct.

Liming material quality is expressed as effective neutralising value, sometimes effective calcium
carbonate equivalent, which combines chemical purity with fineness. Pure calcium carbonate is defined
as 100. Dolomite is chemically about 109 because magnesium carbonate has a lower molecular weight per
unit of neutralising power. Burnt lime, calcium oxide, is about 179 and hydrated lime about 136;
both act fast and both can scorch, so they are unsuited to garden use. Fineness matters as much as
purity: particles coarser than about 2 millimetres react so slowly they are agronomically inert
within the year, which is why a cheap coarse product can be poor value despite a good purity figure.
If a product has an ENV of 75, divide the required pure-limestone rate by 0.75 to get the actual
rate.

For fertiliser, the governing equation is simply the required nutrient divided by the fraction of
that nutrient in the product. Suppose a report calls for 60 kilograms of nitrogen per hectare and the
available product is urea at 46 percent nitrogen. Sixty divided by 0.46 gives 130 kilograms of urea
per hectare. If the same field needs 40 kilograms of P2O5 and the product is triple superphosphate at
46 percent P2O5, that is 87 kilograms per hectare. Where a compound fertiliser is used, one nutrient
will govern and the others will be over- or under-supplied; work out which is limiting, then top up
the deficit with a straight product.

Garden-scale conversion trips people constantly. One kilogram per hectare is 0.1 grams per square
metre, so a field rate of 100 kilograms per hectare is 10 grams per square metre, about two level
teaspoons of a dense granular product. A raised bed of three square metres therefore wants around 30
grams, not the handful that instinct suggests, which is often three to five times too much.

sections.heading: Salinity, Sodium and Contaminants
sections.body:
Beyond nutrients, three categories of soil problem are chemically distinct, frequently confused with
each other, and each requires an entirely different remedy. Getting the diagnosis wrong here wastes
years.

Salinity is an excess of total soluble salts, measured as electrical conductivity of a saturated
paste extract, written ECe and reported in decisiemens per metre, dS/m, numerically the same as the
older millimhos per centimetre. Below about 2 dS/m almost nothing is affected. From 2 to 4, sensitive
crops such as beans, carrots and strawberries lose yield. From 4 to 8, many crops suffer, and above
about 8 only tolerant species such as barley, beet and bermudagrass perform. The mechanism is
osmotic: dissolved salts lower the water potential of the soil solution, so a root must work harder
to extract water, and the plant shows classic drought symptoms in visibly moist soil. Marginal leaf
scorch is typical. The remedy is leaching with good-quality water where drainage permits, which
physically removes the salts, and salinity is by far the more tractable of the two salt problems.

Sodicity is different, and confusing it with salinity leads to the wrong treatment. It is an excess of
sodium relative to calcium and magnesium on the exchange complex, expressed as exchangeable sodium
percentage, ESP, or as the sodium adsorption ratio of the extract. Above roughly 6 percent ESP
structural problems begin, and above 15 percent the soil is formally sodic. The mechanism is
physical: sodium is a large, singly charged, heavily hydrated ion that pushes clay platelets apart
rather than flocculating them, so aggregates disperse into individual particles when wetted. The
result is a soil that seals into an impermeable crust when wet, sets like brick when dry, and sheds
water. Leaching a sodic soil with pure water makes it worse, because removing the remaining salts
accelerates dispersion. The correct treatment supplies calcium to displace sodium, usually gypsum,
calcium sulphate, at several tonnes per hectare, and only then leaches. Gypsum, importantly, does not
change pH, which is why it is not a substitute for lime.

Heavy metals are a health question rather than an agronomic one. Lead is the common one in urban
soils, from paint weathering off older buildings and from decades of leaded petrol. Guidance
thresholds differ between jurisdictions, but total lead below about 100 mg/kg is generally treated as
unrestricted for vegetable growing, 100 to 400 mg/kg as acceptable with precautions, and above about
400 mg/kg as unsuitable for food crops without remediation. The important detail is that most lead
enters the diet as soil dust on produce rather than through the plant, so thorough washing, peeling
root crops, mulching to suppress dust, maintaining pH near 6.5 to 7 and adding organic matter to bind
the metal all reduce exposure substantially. Raised beds with imported soil and a barrier layer are
the definitive answer where levels are high. Arsenic in former orchard land, cadmium from certain
phosphate rock sources, and zinc or copper accumulation from long-term pig or poultry manure are the
other cases worth screening for once.

sections.heading: When the Numbers Look Wrong
sections.body:
A soil report that contradicts what the field is visibly doing is a common and disorienting
experience. In most cases the report is arithmetically correct and something in the chain between
field and number has gone astray. Working through the possibilities in order resolves the great
majority of cases without a second test.

Start with sampling, because it is the largest error source by a wide margin. Cores taken to
inconsistent depths, too few cores, a composite that accidentally included a gateway or a spot where
fertiliser spilled, or a sample taken shortly after applying lime or fertiliser, will all produce a
number that is real but describes something other than the field. Fresh amendment is a particular
trap: a soil sampled two weeks after liming can read a full pH unit above where it will settle,
because the lime is present as undissolved particles that the laboratory's grinding and shaking
dissolve far more efficiently than the field ever will. Allow at least three months, ideally six,
after liming and one month after fertilising.

Next, check whether the problem is physical rather than chemical. If nutrient levels are adequate and
the crop is still poor, the likely culprits are compaction, waterlogging, poor rooting depth or root
disease, none of which a chemical analysis detects. Digging a pit and looking at where roots stop is
more informative than any repeat test. A pan at spade depth, a grey gleyed layer indicating anaerobic
conditions, or roots deflected horizontally will explain what the chemistry cannot.

Consider antagonism and induced deficiency. Nutrients compete for uptake, and an excess of one can
create a functional shortage of another that measures as adequate. Very high potassium suppresses
magnesium uptake and can cause grass tetany in grazing livestock. High phosphorus suppresses zinc.
High calcium reduces uptake of magnesium, potassium and boron. High manganese interferes with iron.
In each case, the soil test for the suppressed nutrient reads acceptable while the plant is
genuinely short, and plant tissue analysis, which measures what actually reached the leaf, is the
tool that settles the question. Tissue testing and soil testing answer different questions and are
complementary rather than competing.

Where a result is truly anomalous, the disciplined response is to resample carefully, submit a
duplicate under a different label to check the laboratory's own reproducibility, and if possible send
a split to a second laboratory using the same method. Genuine laboratory error exists but is rare in
accredited facilities.

Finally, hold the whole enterprise in proportion. A soil test measures chemistry at one moment, in a
disturbed and dried sample, using a proxy extraction calibrated on other people's fields. It is a
strong signal, not a verdict. It cannot see soil biology in any actionable way, cannot see
compaction, cannot predict weather, and cannot know what the crop will actually do. Used alongside a
spade, a record book and honest observation of the growing crop, it is the most cost-effective
instrument in agriculture. Used alone, as an oracle, it will occasionally mislead with great
confidence.

guides.title: Soil Texture, Structure and Tilth
guides.summary: What soil texture, structure and tilth actually are and how they differ: particle size classes and the texture triangle, how to measure texture by feel and by sedimentation, how aggregates form and why they collapse, water retention and compaction, and the practices that genuinely improve soil physical condition as against the ones that do not.

sections.heading: The Physical Condition of Soil Decides Almost Everything
sections.body:
Most people who grow things think about soil in terms of fertility: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium,
pH, whether to add compost or lime. Those matter, but they sit downstream of something more
fundamental. A soil's physical condition - how big its particles are, how they are stuck together, how
much of its volume is empty space and what is in that space - determines whether roots can penetrate,
whether water soaks in or runs off, whether air reaches the root zone, how much water the soil can
hold between rains, how quickly it warms in spring, and whether nutrients that are present are
actually reachable. You can pour fertiliser onto a compacted, structureless soil for years and get
very little back, because the limiting factor was never the nutrient.

Three related ideas organise this whole subject and are constantly confused with one another. Texture
is the proportion of sand, silt and clay particles in a soil. It is set by the parent material and the
weathering history, it is essentially permanent on a human timescale, and you cannot practically
change it. Structure is how those particles are bound together into larger crumbs and blocks called
aggregates or peds, together with the network of pores between them. Structure is created biologically
and destroyed mechanically, it changes over months and years, and it is very much within your control.
Tilth is the working word for the overall physical fitness of the soil for growing: a soil in good
tilth crumbles when handled, takes water readily, and lets a seedling root push through without
effort.

The distinction matters enormously in practice because it tells you which problems are worth
attacking. If your soil is a heavy clay, that is texture, and no amount of intervention will turn it
into loam. But a heavy clay in good structure, with stable crumbs and channels made by roots and
earthworms, can be a superb growing medium: it holds water and nutrients well and drains through the
large pores between aggregates. The same clay compacted and structureless is close to useless, and the
difference between the two is entirely made by management. Conversely a sandy soil will always drain
fast and hold little water, but building organic matter can measurably improve both.

Understanding this system means understanding a chain of causation: mineral particle size sets surface
area and charge, which sets how particles stick together; biology and chemistry then bind them into
aggregates; aggregates create a two-tier pore network; that pore network governs water, air and root
movement; and those in turn govern what will grow. What follows works along that chain, then covers
the practical business of measuring texture in your own field, recognising good and bad structure,
diagnosing compaction, and knowing which soil amendments actually work and which are folklore.

sections.heading: What Soil Is Made Of
sections.body:
A representative topsoil in good condition is, by volume, roughly forty-five per cent mineral matter,
five per cent organic matter, twenty-five per cent water and twenty-five per cent air. The two figures
that surprise people are that half the volume is empty space, and that the organic fraction which does
so much of the work is such a small proportion of the whole.

The mineral fraction is weathered rock. Its composition depends on the parent material - granite,
limestone, shale, volcanic ash, wind-blown loess, river alluvium, glacial till - and on how far
weathering has gone. Quartz, being chemically tough, survives as sand and silt. Feldspars and micas
break down chemically into clay minerals. In the humid tropics, where weathering has run for millions
of years, even the clays have been degraded and what remains is largely iron and aluminium oxides.
Anything larger than 2 millimetres is called coarse fragments or gravel and is excluded from texture
analysis, though it matters practically: a stony soil holds less water simply because the stones
occupy volume.

The organic fraction is a continuum from fresh residue to fully humified material. Fresh residues -
leaves, roots, manure - decompose fast and feed the biology. Partially decomposed material provides the
sticky polysaccharides that glue particles together. Humus, the stable fraction that has resisted
decomposition for decades or centuries, contributes cation exchange capacity, water holding, and
colour. Typical arable topsoil organic matter is 2 to 5 per cent by weight; long-term grassland can
reach 8 to 12 per cent, and peat soils are over 20 per cent by definition. Because organic matter has
a bulk density of only about 0.2 to 0.5 grams per cubic centimetre against about 2.65 for mineral
particles, a small mass fraction occupies a much larger volume fraction than the numbers suggest.

The living fraction is a subset of the organic but deserves separate mention because it does the
engineering. A single gram of healthy topsoil may contain a billion bacteria, several hundred metres of
fungal hyphae, tens of thousands of protozoa and hundreds of nematodes. Earthworm populations in good
pasture can exceed a million per hectare, and their burrows, some of them permanent vertical channels
made by deep-burrowing species, are among the most important pores in the whole profile.

The pore space is what the other fractions leave behind, and it is not one thing. Large pores, above
about 50 micrometres, drain freely under gravity within a day or two and are the ones that carry air.
Medium pores, roughly 0.2 to 50 micrometres, hold the water plants can actually use. Fine pores below
about 0.2 micrometres hold water so tightly that roots cannot extract it. A good soil has a spread of
all three; a compacted or structureless soil has lost most of the large ones.

sections.heading: Sand, Silt and Clay: The Particle Size Classes
sections.body:
Texture is defined entirely by particle size, and the boundaries, though they look arbitrary, mark
real changes in physical behaviour.

Under the USDA system, used across North America and widely elsewhere, sand runs from 2 millimetres
down to 0.05 millimetres, silt from 0.05 down to 0.002 millimetres, and clay is everything below 0.002
millimetres, which is 2 micrometres. Sand is further subdivided into very coarse, coarse, medium, fine
and very fine. The international or ISSS system, used in much of Europe, Australia and by the FAO,
places the sand-silt boundary at 0.02 millimetres rather than 0.05, which means the same soil can be
classified differently depending on which system a laboratory used. This is a genuine and persistent
source of confusion when comparing data across countries, and any texture figure should be read with
its system stated.

The functional differences follow from geometry. Sand particles are large, roughly spherical, and
chemically inert; you can see individual grains, they feel gritty, and they have very little surface
area per unit mass, on the order of 0.01 to 0.1 square metres per gram. Water drains through the wide
gaps between them almost immediately, they hold few nutrients because there is little surface to hold
them on, and they do not stick to each other at all. A pure sand has essentially no structure because
there is nothing to build structure with.

Silt is the same mineralogy, chiefly quartz, at a smaller size. It feels smooth and floury when dry,
slippery but not sticky when wet, roughly like talcum powder. Its surface area is intermediate, around
0.1 to 1 square metre per gram. Silt holds water well in the medium pore range, which makes silty soils
productive, but it has almost no chemical stickiness, so silt-dominated soils have weak structure and
are notoriously prone to surface capping and to erosion. Loess soils, which are wind-deposited silt,
are among the most fertile and the most erodible in the world.

Clay is different in kind, not merely in degree. Below 2 micrometres, particles are typically flat
plates rather than spheres, they are secondary minerals formed by chemical weathering rather than
fragments of the original rock, they carry a net negative electrical charge, and their surface area is
enormous: 10 to 800 square metres per gram depending on mineralogy. A teaspoon of a smectite clay can
have the internal surface area of a football pitch. That surface area and charge is where nutrient
retention, water retention, stickiness, plasticity, shrinking and swelling all come from. Clay is the
active fraction, and a soil's behaviour is dominated by its clay content far out of proportion to the
mass present.

sections.heading: The Texture Triangle and the Twelve Classes
sections.body:
Once you know the percentages of sand, silt and clay, you have a point in a two-dimensional space,
because the three must add to one hundred. The standard way of naming that point is the soil texture
triangle, an equilateral triangle with clay percentage on one axis, silt on another and sand on the
third, divided into twelve named classes. It is a nomenclature, not a theory, but the class boundaries
were drawn where behaviour changes, so the name carries real information.

Reading it is straightforward once you know which way each axis runs. Clay percentage is read along
the left side and its lines run horizontally. Silt is read along the right side with lines running down
and to the left. Sand is read along the base with lines running up and to the left. Find your three
values, follow the corresponding lines, and they intersect at one point in one class. A soil with 40
per cent sand, 40 per cent silt and 20 per cent clay is a loam. Change the clay to 40 per cent and it
becomes a clay loam.

The twelve classes are sand, loamy sand, sandy loam, loam, silt loam, silt, sandy clay loam, clay
loam, silty clay loam, sandy clay, silty clay and clay. Several features of the layout are worth
noticing because they encode the physics. The clay class occupies the top of the triangle and starts
at only 40 per cent clay, whereas sand needs 85 per cent or more to be called a sand. That asymmetry
reflects clay's disproportionate influence: 40 per cent clay is enough to dominate a soil's behaviour,
while 40 per cent sand is not. Similarly, the loam class does not sit at 33 per cent of each. It is
centred nearer 40 per cent sand, 40 per cent silt and 20 per cent clay, because equal thirds would
already behave as a clay loam.

Loam is the word people reach for when they mean good soil, and there is a reason. A loam has enough
sand to drain and warm, enough silt to hold plant-available water, and enough clay to hold nutrients
and bind aggregates, without any one fraction dominating. Sandy loam and silt loam are also excellent
for most purposes. The heavy end of the triangle - clay, silty clay, clay loam - can be highly
productive but demands careful timing, because these soils are workable only within a narrow moisture
window.

Two cautions. First, the triangle describes only the fine earth fraction under 2 millimetres; a soil
called a sandy loam may still be forty per cent stones by volume, which changes everything about how it
behaves in practice. Second, texture is reported per horizon, not per soil. A silt loam topsoil over a
clay subsoil at forty centimetres behaves very differently from a silt loam all the way down, because
the clay layer perches water. Always dig a hole and look at the profile rather than testing only the
surface.

sections.heading: Determining Texture by Feel
sections.body:
The hand texture test is a genuine skill, and an experienced person can place a soil within about five
per cent clay of the laboratory value. It is free, immediate, and can be repeated at every spade depth
and corner of a field, which makes it more useful than a single laboratory number. It
requires a consistent method and calibration against soils you have had analysed.

Each fraction announces itself differently. Sand is felt as grit, individual particles detectable by
rubbing. Silt is felt as smoothness and, when dry, a floury or talc-like quality; wet
silt is slippery but will not hold a shape. Clay is felt as stickiness and, crucially, as plasticity:
only clay lets the soil be moulded and hold the moulded shape. The diagnostic manoeuvre is the ribbon,
in which soil is squeezed between thumb and forefinger and extruded upward, the length it reaches
before breaking under its own weight being roughly proportional to clay content.

Moisture control is the largest source of error. Too dry and clay will not ribbon at all; too wet and
everything becomes slurry. The target is a putty-like consistency where the sample just glistens and
no free water appears under pressure. Add water a few drops at a time and knead thoroughly between
additions, because clay wets slowly and an under-kneaded sample tests low. Remove stones, roots and
organic debris first, since organic matter makes soil feel more silty than it is.

Interpretation has two stages: ribbon length gives the group, and grittiness or smoothness gives the
member within it. A useful cross-check is the shine test - rub a wetted sample with a thumbnail, and
the more clay, the more it takes a waxy polish. A pure silt takes none at all.
steps: Take a tablespoon of soil from the horizon you want to assess, discarding stones over 2 mm, roots and residue.
Wet it a few drops at a time, kneading thoroughly after each addition, until it reaches a putty-like consistency that just glistens but releases no free water.
Try to roll it into a ball about 25 mm across. If it will not form a ball at all, it is a sand; if it forms a very fragile ball, it is a loamy sand, and you can stop here.
If a ball forms, squeeze the soil upward between thumb and forefinger to extrude a ribbon over the edge of the finger, letting it emerge under its own weight rather than pushing it out flat.
Measure the ribbon length at the point it breaks: under 25 mm indicates the loam group, 25 to 50 mm the clay loam group, over 50 mm the clay group.
Wet a small pinch heavily and rub it between the fingers: distinct grittiness makes it the sandy member of that group, distinct smoothness the silty member, neither the plain member.
Confirm with the shine test - rub a wet sample with a thumbnail; a waxy polish indicates high clay, none indicates silt or sand.
Repeat on three samples from the same horizon and take the consensus, then repeat at each layer down the profile.

sections.heading: Measuring Texture by Sedimentation
sections.body:
The laboratory method rests on Stokes' law, which states that a particle falling through a fluid
reaches a terminal velocity proportional to the square of its diameter. A sand grain of 0.05
millimetres falls about six hundred times faster than a clay particle of 0.002 millimetres. Disperse a
soil in water, let it settle, and the fractions separate in order; by sampling the suspension at
known times and depths you can calculate their proportions.

The hydrometer method measures suspension density with a calibrated float at 40 seconds, when sand has
settled and the reading gives silt plus clay, and again at 2 or 7 hours, when only clay remains. The pipette method withdraws a known volume from a set depth, dries it and weighs it. Both require complete dispersion first, which
means destroying the aggregates you spend the rest of your life trying to build: samples are treated
with hydrogen peroxide to remove organic matter, then with a dispersant, and shaken for minutes. Skipping dispersion is the classic error: clay is
then counted as silt because it is still glued into crumbs.

Modern laboratories increasingly use laser diffraction, which is fast but systematically reports less
clay than sedimentation, because clay plates are flat and laser methods assume spheres.

The kitchen version, the jar test, is a genuine sedimentation analysis at low precision and is worth
doing. Its accuracy is limited by incomplete dispersion and by the difficulty of seeing the sand-silt
boundary, and it tends to overestimate silt at the expense of clay. Treat it as a class check, not a
number.
ingredients: A straight-sided clear jar of at least 1 litre with a tight lid, with a ruler taped alongside.
About 250 millilitres of air-dried soil from a single horizon, sieved through a 2 mm kitchen sieve to remove stones and roots.
Distilled or rainwater if available, since hard tap water contains calcium that will flocculate clay and ruin the separation.
A dispersing agent: 5 millilitres of dishwasher rinse aid, or 5 grams of sodium hexametaphosphate - check the label, as many products have been reformulated.
A permanent marker and a notebook.
steps: Half-fill the jar with sieved soil, then add water to about 80 per cent full, leaving air space for shaking.
Add the dispersing agent, seal the lid and shake hard for a full 3 to 5 minutes; under-shaking is the commonest cause of a wrong answer.
Set the jar on a level surface where it will not be disturbed and start timing.
At 40 seconds, mark the top of the settled layer: everything below that line is sand.
At 2 hours, mark the new top of the settled layer: the band between the first and second marks is silt.
Leave undisturbed for 24 to 48 hours until the water clears, then mark the final level: the band between the second and third marks is clay.
Measure each band in millimetres, divide each by the total settled depth and multiply by 100 to obtain percentages, which should sum to 100.
Plot the three percentages on a texture triangle to read off the class, and repeat for each horizon.

sections.heading: Clay Mineralogy: Why Clay Behaves As It Does
sections.body:
Two soils with identical clay percentages can behave completely differently, and the reason is
mineralogy. Clay minerals are layered aluminosilicates built from two kinds of sheet: a tetrahedral
sheet of silicon and oxygen, and an octahedral sheet of aluminium, oxygen and hydroxyl. How these
sheets are stacked defines the mineral and, through it, the soil's engineering properties.

Kaolinite is a 1:1 mineral, one tetrahedral sheet bonded to one octahedral sheet, with the layers held
together by strong hydrogen bonds. Water cannot get between the layers, so kaolinite does not swell.
Its surface area is modest, 10 to 30 square metres per gram, and its cation exchange capacity - the
amount of positively charged nutrient it can hold - is low, about 3 to 15 centimoles of charge per
kilogram. Kaolinitic soils dominate the humid tropics and the older landscapes of the southeastern
United States and are relatively easy to work but poor at holding nutrients.

Smectite, of which montmorillonite is the best-known member, is a 2:1 mineral, an octahedral sheet
sandwiched between two tetrahedral sheets, with only weak bonds between the sandwiches. Water and
cations move freely into that interlayer space, so the mineral swells dramatically when wet and shrinks
when dry. Surface area reaches 600 to 800 square metres per gram counting internal surfaces, and cation
exchange capacity runs 80 to 150 centimoles per kilogram. Smectitic soils, called Vertisols when
smectite dominates, are the cracking clays of the Indian Deccan, the Australian downs and the Texas
blackland prairie. They are chemically rich, physically brutal to manage, and swell so strongly that
they crack buildings and break roads.

Illite sits between the two: a 2:1 structure like smectite but with potassium ions locked in the
interlayer holding it shut, giving intermediate surface area of 70 to 120 square metres per gram and
exchange capacity of 20 to 40. Vermiculite is 2:1 with limited swelling and high exchange capacity.
Iron and aluminium oxides such as goethite and gibbsite are not layer silicates at all; they carry
variable charge that turns positive under acid conditions and act as powerful cementing agents, which
is why deeply weathered tropical soils often have remarkably stable aggregates despite low organic
matter.

The practical significance is that shrink-swell behaviour is a mineralogy question, not a texture
question. A soil that develops deep cracks in dry weather is telling you it is smectitic. Those cracks
are a genuine mixed blessing: they let irrigation water bypass the root zone entirely through preferential
flow, and they shear roots, but they also self-repair compaction, because the swelling and shrinking
cycle is nature's own subsoiler. A kaolinitic clay of the same texture will not crack, will not
self-repair, and will hold a compaction pan indefinitely once you have made one.

sections.heading: From Texture to Structure: Aggregates and Peds
sections.body:
Structure is what happens when individual particles are bound into larger units. Those units, called
aggregates when discussing the process and peds when describing the field morphology, are the
functional building blocks of soil, and the spaces between them matter as much as the units
themselves.

Field descriptions classify peds by shape, size and how distinctly they are developed. Granular
structure consists of roughly spherical crumbs 1 to 10 millimetres across, held together by roots and
organic glues; it is the classic signature of a healthy topsoil under grass and is what everyone is
aiming for. Blocky structure gives angular or subangular blocks 5 to 50 millimetres, typical of clay-
rich B horizons and acceptable if the blocks are small and the faces are not shiny. Prismatic
structure forms vertical columns with flat tops, common in clay subsoils and in soils that shrink and
swell. Columnar structure is prismatic with rounded tops and is diagnostic of sodium-affected soils.
Platy structure, in which the units are horizontal plates, is nearly always a warning sign: it forms
under compaction from wheels or hooves, or beneath a plough, and it obstructs both drainage and root
growth because the plate faces are horizontal barriers. Two conditions count as structureless: single
grain, where particles do not stick at all, as in a clean sand, and massive, where the soil is a
coherent lump with no planes of weakness, which is the condition of a severely degraded clay.

The mechanism of aggregation is hierarchical, a model developed by John Tisdall and Malcolm Oades in
1982 and still the standard framework. At the smallest scale, below about 2 micrometres, clay plates
and organic molecules bind through electrostatic attraction and polyvalent cation bridges, chiefly
calcium, which links a negatively charged clay surface to a negatively charged organic molecule.
These build into microaggregates of 20 to 250 micrometres, held by persistent organic matter and iron
and aluminium oxides. Microaggregates are stable and largely resistant to management. Above 250
micrometres, macroaggregates are bound by transient and temporary agents: fungal hyphae and fine roots
that physically enmesh them, and microbial polysaccharides that glue them.

That hierarchy has a direct management implication. Macroaggregates depend on living, actively growing
biology and on continuous inputs of fresh organic matter, so they build within a season or two and are
lost within a season or two. Microaggregates depend on chemistry and slow-cycling organic matter, and
take decades to build or destroy. When you damage a soil's structure by tillage or traffic, you mostly
destroy the macroaggregates first, which is why the loss is fast and the recovery, if you stop, is also
reasonably fast. It also explains why a soil can look transformed after one season of cover cropping
and yet still be fundamentally fragile underneath.

sections.heading: Porosity, Bulk Density and the Movement of Water and Air
sections.body:
The reason structure matters is that it creates pore space of the right sizes in the right
arrangement. Two measurements capture this: porosity, the fraction of soil volume that is pore, and
bulk density, the mass of dry soil per unit of total volume including pores.

Bulk density is measured by driving a ring of known volume into undisturbed soil, drying the contents
at 105 degrees Celsius until constant mass, and dividing. Since mineral particles have a particle
density near 2.65 grams per cubic centimetre, porosity can be calculated as one minus bulk density
divided by 2.65. A well-structured loam topsoil has a bulk density around 1.1 to 1.4 grams per cubic
centimetre, giving about 47 to 58 per cent porosity. Sandy soils naturally run higher, 1.4 to 1.6,
because sand grains pack efficiently and there is little organic matter; clays in good structure run
lower, 1.0 to 1.3. The thresholds that matter are the root-limiting ones: roughly 1.8 for sands, 1.65
for loams and 1.47 for clays. Above those figures, root elongation is severely restricted regardless of
water and nutrients.

Water moves through soil by two distinct mechanisms. Saturated flow, when all pores are full, is driven
by gravity and by pressure differences, and it happens almost entirely through the largest pores.
Because flow rate through a cylindrical pore scales with the fourth power of its radius, a single
1 millimetre earthworm channel conducts as much water as roughly ten thousand pores of 0.1 millimetres.
This is why saturated hydraulic conductivity depends overwhelmingly on structure rather than texture,
and why a well-aggregated clay can drain faster than a structureless silt. Unsaturated flow, once the
large pores have drained, is driven by capillary suction and moves through the smaller pores and along
water films; it is slow, and it moves in any direction including upward.

Air occupies whatever the water leaves. Roots and aerobic microbes consume oxygen and produce carbon
dioxide, and gas exchange with the atmosphere occurs mainly by diffusion through continuous air-filled
pores. The practical threshold is air-filled porosity of about 10 per cent of soil volume: below that,
oxygen supply becomes limiting, root respiration falls, nutrient uptake slows, and after a day or two
denitrifying bacteria begin converting nitrate to nitrogen gas and losing it to the atmosphere. This
is why waterlogging kills plants; they do not drown in the water, they suffocate in the absence of air.

A useful way to hold all this together is that texture sets the range of pore sizes available and
structure decides how much of that range you actually get. A clay has, in principle, an enormous
number of fine pores and very few large ones; aggregation converts some of that fine-pore mass into
crumbs with large channels between them, and compaction converts it straight back. Sand has the
opposite problem, plenty of large pores and almost no medium ones, which is why organic matter is the
only lever that improves a sand and why its effect there is proportionally so large.

sections.heading: Water Retention: Field Capacity, Wilting Point and Available Water
sections.body:
How much water a soil can supply to a crop between rains is one of the most useful numbers in
agriculture, and it follows directly from texture and structure through the physics of capillarity.

Water is held in soil against gravity by surface tension and by adsorption onto particle surfaces. The
tension is expressed as a negative pressure or suction, conventionally in units of bar, kilopascals or
pF. Immediately after heavy rain the soil is saturated at zero suction. Over the next one to three days
gravity drains the largest pores, and the soil arrives at field capacity, conventionally defined as a
suction of about 0.33 bar, or 33 kilopascals, in medium-textured soils and about 0.1 bar in sands. As
roots extract water the suction rises until, at about 15 bar or 1,500 kilopascals, most crop plants can
no longer pull water out and wilt without recovering overnight. That is the permanent wilting point.
The water held between those two suctions is the plant-available water capacity, and it is the only
water that matters agronomically.

The numbers follow texture in a pattern that is not intuitive. Sand has low field capacity, around 10
per cent by volume, and very low wilting point, around 4 per cent, so available water is only about 6
per cent, or 6 millimetres per 100 millimetres of soil depth. Clay holds far more total water, with
field capacity around 40 per cent, but its wilting point is also very high, around 25 per cent, because
much of that water is in fine pores at suctions no root can overcome. Available water in a clay is
therefore about 15 per cent. Loam and silt loam are the winners, with field capacity about 32 per cent,
wilting point about 12 per cent and available water around 20 per cent, or 200 millimetres in a metre of
rooting depth. This is the physical reason silt loam is prized: it has the largest fraction of pores in
the size range that holds water loosely enough for roots to get it back.

Organic matter improves the picture at both ends. Each one per cent increase in soil organic matter is
commonly cited as adding roughly 10 to 25 millimetres of available water per metre of soil, though
published estimates vary widely and the effect is proportionally much larger in sands than in clays.
The often-repeated figure of 20,000 gallons per acre per one per cent is at the extreme optimistic end
of the literature and should be treated with caution.

Total available water to a crop is the available water capacity multiplied by rooting depth, which is
why compaction is so damaging: halving effective rooting depth halves the drought reserve regardless of
how good the topsoil is. A crop rooting to one metre in a loam has about 200 millimetres in store,
roughly three weeks of summer demand. The same crop rooting only to 30 centimetres because of a plough
pan has 60 millimetres, or about a week.

sections.heading: Tilth: What Good Physical Condition Looks Like
sections.body:
Tilth is the practical, sensory summary of everything else. It has no single instrument reading, which
makes some scientists uncomfortable, but experienced growers assess it reliably and consistently, and
the indicators map onto measurable properties.

A soil in good tilth crumbles under gentle pressure into rounded aggregates of two to ten millimetres
rather than shattering into dust or breaking into hard clods. It is dark, because of organic matter,
