per hectare per year. Against that, a bare, sloping, conventionally ploughed field can shed 10, 40 or in
extreme storm events several hundred tonnes per hectare in a single season. The arithmetic is not subtle. A
field losing 20 tonnes per hectare annually is losing about 1.5 millimetres of depth each year, and a soil
with 25 centimetres of topsoil over hostile subsoil has fewer than two centuries of farming left in it at
that rate — far less once yields begin to fall partway down.

What makes erosion insidious is that it is selective and gradual. Running water does not take a uniform slice.
It preferentially carries away the lightest, finest fraction: clay particles, silt, and the organic colloids
that hold nutrients and water. The material left behind is coarser, poorer in nitrogen, phosphorus and carbon,
and less able to store moisture. This is why an eroding field can look normal for a decade while its yield
slowly stiffens against fertiliser, and why the sediment leaving it is roughly two to five times richer in
nutrients than the soil it came from — a ratio soil scientists call the enrichment ratio. The loss is
therefore doubly expensive: the field is impoverished and the receiving stream is fertilised, which is a
principal driver of algal blooms and low-oxygen dead zones downstream.

The consequences reach past the farm gate. Sediment fills reservoirs and shortens their design lives, chokes
irrigation canals, smothers the gravel beds where fish spawn, and raises the cost of drinking-water treatment.
Wind-borne soil abrades seedlings, buries fences, degrades air quality and carries the fine particulate matter
that aggravates asthma. During the North American Dust Bowl of the 1930s, roughly 3.5 million people left the
southern Great Plains, and a single storm on 11 May 1934 carried an estimated 300 million tonnes of soil east
as far as ships several hundred kilometres out in the Atlantic.

The encouraging half of the story is that erosion is one of the best-understood and most reliably fixable
problems in land management. It obeys straightforward physics, it responds to a small number of well-tested
interventions, and most of those interventions are cheap, use materials already present on the site, and pay
for themselves in retained fertility and water. Nearly every effective technique reduces to one of three
principles: keep the soil covered, slow the water down, and give the soil the structure to absorb rain rather
than shed it. Everything else is detail about how to accomplish those three things on a particular slope, in a
particular climate, with a particular set of tools.

sections.heading: What Soil Is Made Of and Why It Comes Apart
sections.body:
To understand why soil moves, it helps to know what holds it together. Mineral soil is a mixture of particles
sorted by size: sand from 2 millimetres down to 0.05 millimetres, silt from 0.05 down to 0.002 millimetres,
and clay below 0.002 millimetres. Sand grains are essentially tiny rocks — inert, heavy, and cohesionless.
Clay particles are plate-like crystals with electrically charged surfaces; they attract water and each other,
and they are the chief source of a soil's stickiness. Silt sits awkwardly in between: too fine to be heavy,
too coarse to be cohesive. Silt-dominated soils, particularly the wind-deposited loess soils of the American
Midwest, northern Europe and the Loess Plateau of China, are among the most erodible on Earth, which is
precisely why those regions have historically suffered the most spectacular gullying.

Individual particles rarely act alone in a healthy soil. They are bound into crumbs and clods called
aggregates by four main glues. Clay bridges hold particles by electrostatic attraction. Iron and aluminium
oxides act as chemical cements, which is why many tropical red soils resist slaking despite heavy rain. Roots
and fungal hyphae — especially the threads of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi — physically enmesh particles like
reinforcing mesh in concrete. And microbial and root exudates, notably polysaccharide gums and a glycoprotein
family associated with mycorrhizae, glue the mesh together. The result is a soil built of porous crumbs
typically 1 to 5 millimetres across, with large pores between them for air and rapid drainage and small pores
within them for stored water.

Erosion begins when that architecture fails. The dominant failure mode in the field is slaking: a dry
aggregate is wetted suddenly, air trapped inside is compressed by advancing water, and the aggregate bursts
from within. You can watch this in three minutes on a kitchen table by dropping a dry clod into a glass of
water — a well-aggregated soil holds its shape and merely darkens, while a degraded one collapses into a cloudy
heap. A second mode is dispersion, in which clay platelets repel one another and drift apart in water. Sodium
is the main culprit: a soil with a high proportion of exchangeable sodium (broadly, above about 6 per cent of
exchange sites, defining a sodic soil) disperses readily, seals its surface, and erodes catastrophically. Gypsum,
which supplies calcium to displace sodium, is the standard remedy at typical rates of 2 to 10 tonnes per hectare.

Once aggregates fail, the freed fines wash into surface pores and form a seal only a millimetre or two thick.
When that seal dries it becomes a crust that can cut the soil's water intake rate by 80 to 90 per cent. Rain
that would have soaked in now runs off instead, and the field has moved from absorbing its weather to shedding
it. Almost every good conservation practice is, at bottom, an attempt to prevent that first millimetre from
sealing.

sections.heading: The Physics of Water Erosion: Splash, Sheet and Flow
sections.body:
Water erosion is a two-stage process — detachment then transport — and each stage is driven by a different
form of energy. Detachment on the open field is dominated not by flowing water but by the impact of individual
raindrops. A large drop 5 millimetres across reaches a terminal velocity near 9 metres per second and strikes
bare soil with enough kinetic energy to blast particles up to 60 centimetres sideways and a few centimetres into
the air. Across a hectare, a single intense storm delivers on the order of 100 to 200 megajoules of impact
energy. That is the reason bare soil erodes so much more than covered soil even where runoff volumes are
similar: cover intercepts the drops before they land, and a mulch layer or a dense canopy near the ground can
cut splash detachment by 90 per cent or more.

Transport then depends on flowing water. Once rainfall exceeds the soil's infiltration rate, water ponds in
surface depressions and, when those fill, begins to move as a thin sheet a few millimetres deep. This sheet
flow is slow and carries mainly what splash has already loosened. But sheet flow is unstable. Tiny
irregularities concentrate it into threads, the threads deepen, and within a few tens of metres downslope it
has organised itself into rills — small channels, typically 5 to 30 centimetres deep, that can be erased by a
single pass of tillage. In rills the water is deeper and faster, and its capacity to both detach and carry
soil rises steeply.

The steepness of that rise is the key quantitative fact of the whole subject. The mass of sediment flowing
water can carry scales roughly with the fifth power of its velocity, and the size of the largest particle it
can move scales with roughly the sixth power. Doubling velocity therefore multiplies transport capacity about
thirty-twofold. Slope enters through velocity: for a given depth and roughness, the Manning equation gives
velocity proportional to the square root of the slope gradient, so a 9 per cent slope moves water about 1.7
times faster than a 3 per cent slope and can carry an order of magnitude more sediment. Slope length matters
too, because a longer slope accumulates more runoff into the same channel; erosion rate typically rises with
slope length to a power of about 0.4 to 0.5 on gentle land and closer to 0.6 on steep land.

Three practical consequences follow directly. First, anything that slows water — roughness, vegetation,
contour ridges, check structures — reduces erosion far more than intuition suggests, because of that fifth-power
relationship. Second, breaking a long slope into short ones with terraces or diversions is powerful even when
the gradient is unchanged, because it stops runoff accumulating. Third, protecting the surface from drop impact
attacks the problem at the detachment stage, before transport ever has anything to carry. Good practice usually
does all three at once.

sections.heading: Reading the Ground: Sheet, Rill, Gully and Streambank
sections.body:
Diagnosing erosion in the field is a skill of reading small evidence, because by the time damage is obvious the
cheap remedies have often been passed. The mildest form, interrill or sheet erosion, removes a thin, fairly
uniform layer and leaves few dramatic signs. Look instead for pedestals: small columns of soil capped and
protected by a pebble or a plant crown, standing one or two centimetres proud of the surrounding surface. That
height is the depth already lost. Look for exposed plant crowns and roots, for a paler subsoil colour showing
on knolls and shoulder slopes while the footslopes darken, and for fans of fine soil deposited against fence
lines, at field edges or on road shoulders after a storm. Sheet erosion is the largest cumulative loss in most
farmed landscapes precisely because it is the least visible.

Rills are the next stage and the most useful diagnostic. They are channels roughly ankle-deep or less that a
tillage pass will obliterate, and they mark exactly where concentrated flow forms. Counting and measuring them
gives a genuine number: measure the average cross-sectional area in square centimetres, multiply by the length
in metres and by the number of rills, and convert using a bulk density near 1.3 tonnes per cubic metre. Ten
rills 15 centimetres wide and 8 centimetres deep running 100 metres across a hectare represent about 15 tonnes
of soil — a serious annual loss from a single storm. Note where they start, because that upslope point is where
flow first becomes erosive and is where a diversion or a strip of permanent cover will do the most good.

Gullies are channels too deep to cross with machinery, conventionally deeper than about 30 centimetres, and
they behave differently. A gully is not simply a large rill; it is a small stream in the making. It advances by
headcutting, where water plunging over the vertical lip at its upper end undermines the base, the lip collapses,
and the whole gully marches upslope, sometimes several metres in a single wet season. Because a headcut is
driven by the plunge, the effective repair is almost always to control the water arriving at the head, not to
fill the gully and hope.

Streambank and channel erosion completes the sequence. Banks fail by a combination of toe scour, in which
current removes support from the base until the mass above collapses, and by rapid drawdown, in which a saturated
bank slumps when the water level in the channel falls quickly after a flood. In many watersheds, streambanks
contribute a surprisingly large share — often 30 to 60 per cent — of the total sediment reaching a river, which
means upland practices alone will not fix a turbid stream if the channel itself is unstable.

A practical habit is to walk the same route after every large storm, always in the same direction, and
photograph the same three or four fixed points. Erosion is a slow accumulation of episodic events, and memory is
an unreliable instrument for measuring it. Photographs from the same spot across five years reveal trends that
no single visit can.

sections.heading: Wind Erosion: Saltation, Suspension and Surface Creep
sections.body:
Wind moves soil by a different mechanism from water, and the difference dictates the remedies. Wind exerts a
shearing drag on the surface, and that drag must exceed a threshold before any grain moves. The threshold is a
function of grain size, and it has a distinctive minimum: particles around 0.1 millimetre in diameter — fine
sand — are the easiest of all to lift, moving at wind speeds near the ground of about 4 to 6 metres per second,
equivalent to roughly 20 kilometres per hour measured at the standard 2-metre height. Coarser grains are too
heavy. Finer particles, counterintuitively, are harder to start because they lie within the still boundary
layer close to the surface and are held by cohesion. This is why bare dune sand blows readily while a smooth
clay pan may sit still in the same wind, and why the fine dust that ends up in the atmosphere is usually not
lifted directly but knocked loose by something coarser.

That knocking is saltation, the engine of the whole process. A fine sand grain rises steeply, follows a low
arc typically 20 to 50 centimetres high, and returns at a shallow angle with enough momentum to eject several
more grains on impact. The result is a self-amplifying chain reaction that reaches full development over a
downwind distance of roughly 50 to 100 metres of bare, erodible surface. Saltation accounts for perhaps 50 to
70 per cent of the total mass moved and does most of the abrasive damage to seedlings, since a young plant is
sandblasted at knee height rather than buried. Above saltation, particles finer than about 0.1 millimetre that
have been dislodged go into suspension and can travel hundreds or thousands of kilometres; this fraction is
usually 3 to 40 per cent of the mass but carries most of the organic matter and nutrients. Below, grains
coarser than about 0.5 millimetre are too heavy to leave the ground and roll and slide along in surface creep,
perhaps 5 to 25 per cent of the total.

The control logic follows from the mechanism. Because saltation needs an unobstructed fetch to build, shortening
the fetch is powerful: barriers, strips of standing crop, or roughness elements placed across the prevailing
wind interrupt the chain reaction before it matures. Because the threshold depends on what the wind actually
touches, anything that lifts the drag away from loose grains works — standing stubble, clods, gravel, a crust
of moist soil, or growing plants. And because moisture raises the threshold sharply, a soil at or above about 4
to 6 per cent gravimetric moisture in its top centimetre is largely immune until it dries.

Risk is therefore highest in a predictable window: a fine-textured or sandy soil, recently tilled to a smooth
finish, dry at the surface, with little residue, exposed to a long uninterrupted fetch, in the season before a
canopy closes. Almost every serious wind erosion event in agricultural history has occurred in exactly that
combination of conditions, and each of the five factors can be altered independently.

sections.heading: Tillage Erosion: The Loss Nobody Sees
sections.body:
There is a third form of soil movement that leaves no muddy water and no dust cloud, and which for most of the
twentieth century went entirely unrecognised. Tillage erosion is the net downslope translocation of soil by
implements. Every pass of a plough, disc, cultivator or even a rotary hoe throws soil a short distance. On level
ground the throw is symmetrical and nothing is lost. On a slope, gravity biases the throw: soil moved downhill
travels farther than soil moved uphill, and the difference accumulates pass after pass, year after year.

The magnitude is larger than most people expect. Measured rates on rolling cropland commonly fall between 10 and
60 tonnes per hectare per year on convex hilltops and shoulder slopes, comparable to or greater than water
erosion on the same fields. A mouldboard plough working across a 10 per cent slope typically moves soil a net 3
to 8 centimetres downhill per pass; a heavy chisel or disc pass moves somewhat less; a rotary tiller in a
market garden, oddly, can move a great deal because of the violence of its throw. The rate scales roughly
linearly with slope gradient, with tillage depth, and with speed, so a deep, fast pass on a steep bank is the
worst case.

The signature of tillage erosion is diagnostic and quite different from water's. Water erosion produces losses
concentrated in flow paths and hollows. Tillage erosion produces losses concentrated on convexities — hilltops,
crests, the shoulders where a slope steepens — and deposition on concavities, in hollows and at the base of
slopes where the gradient flattens. Walk a rolling field in early spring and the pattern shows plainly as pale,
subsoil-coloured caps on every knoll with dark, deep accumulations in every swale. Where fields have been ploughed
for generations along a fixed boundary, soil piles against the downslope hedge or fence in a bank called a
lynchet or a tillage terrace, sometimes a metre or more high; these features are common in long-farmed parts of
Europe and are direct measurements of centuries of implement-driven movement.

The consequences are the same as for water erosion but distributed differently: thin, droughty, low-yielding
knolls that respond poorly to fertiliser, and over-thick, sometimes waterlogged hollows. Because the soil is not
leaving the field, it does not appear in water-quality monitoring and is entirely absent from the standard
erosion prediction equations, which model water only. Yield maps from combine harvesters have made the pattern
newly visible, and the correlation between the pale-knoll pattern and depressed yield is usually strong.

The remedies are structural rather than protective. Reducing tillage intensity and depth cuts the rate roughly
proportionally, and no-till reduces it essentially to zero. Where tillage continues, working along the contour
rather than up and down at least prevents the systematic downhill bias from compounding, though it does not
eliminate lateral throw. Lifting implements at headlands, avoiding tillage on the steepest convexities, and
returning soil upslope periodically with a blade are practical if laborious fixes for small, valuable plots.

sections.heading: Predicting Loss: The Universal Soil Loss Equation and Its Successors
sections.body:
The most influential tool in the field is a deceptively simple product of six factors, developed by Walter
Wischmeier and Dwight Smith from more than 10,000 plot-years of United States runoff data and published in its
mature form in 1965 and 1978. The Universal Soil Loss Equation states that average annual soil loss A equals R
times K times L times S times C times P. Each term isolates one influence, and learning what each represents
matters more than memorising the formula, because the factors are how practitioners think about the problem
even when they never do the arithmetic.

R is rainfall erosivity, a climate term computed from the energy and the maximum 30-minute intensity of storms.
It varies enormously: roughly 500 to 1,000 in metric units across drier temperate regions, 3,000 to 6,000 along
the humid Gulf Coast, and above 10,000 in parts of the wet
tropics. K is soil erodibility, an empirically measured property reflecting texture, organic matter, structure
and permeability; values run from about 0.02 for a well-aggregated clay or a stony soil to 0.06 or higher for a
bare silt loam. L and S are slope length and steepness, usually combined; they are computed relative to a
standard plot 22.1 metres long at 9 per cent slope. C is the cover and management factor, the ratio of loss under
a given cropping system to loss from continuously bare, tilled fallow. P is the support-practice factor, covering
contouring, strip cropping and terracing.

The point of the structure is that C and P are the terms a manager controls, and they have the widest range.
R, K, L and S might vary by a factor of ten across a region. C varies by a factor of a thousand.
Continuous bare fallow is 1.0 by definition. Conventionally tilled continuous row crop typically runs 0.3 to 0.5.
A good rotation with winter cover might reach 0.05 to 0.15. No-till with heavy residue can reach 0.02 to 0.05.
Permanent well-managed pasture is around 0.01, and undisturbed forest floor around 0.001 to 0.005. P is more
modest: contouring alone gives roughly 0.5 to 0.6 on moderate slopes, contour strip cropping 0.25 to 0.4, and
well-designed terraces with grassed outlets 0.1 to 0.2.

Successors have refined the machinery without changing the logic. RUSLE and RUSLE2 replaced the empirical tables
with continuous functions, added sub-factors for surface roughness and prior land use, and handle complex slopes.
WEPP and its European relatives abandon the empirical form and simulate detachment, transport and deposition
process by process, predicting where sediment is deposited rather than only how much leaves.

Two honest cautions apply. These models estimate long-term averages, not the loss from any particular storm, and
their uncertainty on an individual field is easily plus or minus 50 per cent. And they were built on plot data,
so they describe sheet and rill erosion only — they do not model gully erosion, tillage erosion or streambank
failure, which in some catchments dominate the total. Use them to compare management options on the same field,
which is what they do well, rather than to certify an absolute number.

sections.heading: Cover: The Single Most Powerful Control
sections.body:
If a reader takes one principle away, it should be this: keeping living or dead plant material on the soil
surface does more to prevent erosion than every structural measure combined, and it is usually the cheapest thing
available. The relationship between surface cover and soil loss is not linear but exponential, and the shape of
that curve is the most useful practical fact in the discipline. Roughly, relative soil loss falls as the
exponential of a negative constant times percentage cover, with the constant near 0.035 for typical crop residues.
In plain terms, 20 per cent cover cuts loss by about half. Forty per cent cover cuts it by roughly 70 per cent.
Sixty per cent cover cuts it by about 85 to 90 per cent. Above 80 per cent the curve flattens and further gains are
small.

That shape has a decisive management implication. The most valuable increment of cover is the first — going from
bare to 30 per cent achieves more than going from 60 to 90. A grower who cannot achieve full residue cover
everywhere should therefore spread a modest amount of cover widely rather than concentrating a thick mulch on a
small area. And a field that is 90 per cent covered but has a bare 10 per cent occupying a concentrated flow path
is not 90 per cent protected, because the bare strip is exactly where the water is.

Cover works through several distinct mechanisms, which is why it is so robust. It intercepts raindrop energy
before impact, eliminating splash detachment. It physically obstructs and slows overland flow, raising surface
roughness — Manning's roughness coefficient rises from about 0.01 on bare smooth soil to 0.04 or more with heavy
residue, and since velocity falls in proportion to roughness while transport capacity scales with roughly the
fifth power of velocity, that change alone is transformative. It maintains infiltration by preventing the surface
seal from forming, so less water runs off in the first place. It moderates surface temperature and evaporation,
keeping the top centimetre moist and cohesive against wind. And as it decomposes it feeds the soil biology that
builds aggregates.

Height matters less than proximity to the ground. A tall crop canopy is far less protective than intuition
suggests, because drops that coalesce on leaves and fall from two metres regain most of their terminal velocity
and may strike harder than the original rain. This is why erosion under mature maize or under a plantation canopy
with bare floor can be severe, and why a low understorey, a cover crop between rows, or a residue layer is what
actually protects. In forestry and orchard systems the litter layer, not the trees, is the erosion control.

Sources of cover are correspondingly varied: crop residue left standing or flat, a cover crop drilled after
harvest, a living mulch grown between rows, imported straw or wood chip, gravel on paths, or geotextile matting on
newly disturbed slopes. The mechanism is identical in every case.

sections.heading: Residue Management, Reduced Tillage and No-Till
sections.body:
Tillage is the practice that most reliably creates erodible conditions, because it buries the residue that would
protect the surface, destroys aggregates by mechanical shearing, and leaves a fine, loose seedbed with no
cohesion. A mouldboard plough followed by two secondary passes typically leaves under 10 per cent surface cover.
The spectrum of alternatives is best understood as a gradient of decreasing disturbance, each rung leaving more
residue and losing less soil.

Reduced or conservation tillage is conventionally defined as any system leaving at least 30 per cent of the
surface covered by residue after planting, which as a rule of thumb cuts soil loss by 50 to 70 per cent relative
to clean tillage. Chisel ploughing fractures the soil with narrow shanks rather than inverting it and typically
leaves 30 to 50 per cent cover. Disc systems leave less, perhaps 20 to 40 per cent, because the concave blades
partially bury residue. Ridge-till builds permanent ridges, plants into their scraped tops and leaves residue in
the furrows. Strip-till disturbs only a band 15 to 25 centimetres wide where the seed goes, leaving the interrow
untouched — a good compromise in cold, wet springs where full no-till soils warm too slowly.

No-till places seed directly into undisturbed soil through the residue, using a coulter to cut a slot and press
wheels to close it. Where it is well executed, soil loss commonly falls by 90 to 98 per cent relative to
conventional tillage, infiltration rises substantially as continuous earthworm and root channels survive from year
to year, and tillage erosion goes to essentially zero. Long-term no-till fields typically develop a distinct
stratification, with organic matter concentrating in the top 5 centimetres, higher earthworm populations — often
several hundred per square metre against a few dozen under the plough — and much greater aggregate stability.

The honest difficulties deserve equal billing, because oversold no-till fails and gets abandoned. Residue keeps
soils cold and wet, which can delay spring emergence by a week or more in northern climates and reduce yield in
cold years. Weed control shifts from mechanical to chemical or to cover-crop suppression, which is a genuine
constraint for organic systems, though roller-crimped cover crops and precision inter-row cultivation have made
low-disturbance organic production increasingly workable. Surface-applied phosphorus can stratify and move in
dissolved form in runoff even as sediment loss falls, so nutrient placement below the surface matters. Compaction
must be managed by controlled traffic rather than by ripping it out each year. And no-till is a system, not an
implement: it takes three to five years for soil structure and biology to reorganise, and yields often dip
slightly during that transition before recovering and surpassing the old system.

The general rule is to reduce disturbance as far as the operation can genuinely sustain, rather than adopting
the most extreme option and reverting after one bad season.

sections.heading: Contouring, Strip Cropping and Rotation
sections.body:
Cultivating across a slope rather than up and down it is the oldest and cheapest support practice, and its logic
is simple: every furrow, wheel track and ridge becomes a small dam that holds water where it falls instead of
channelling it downhill. On a moderate slope, contour tillage alone typically halves soil loss, corresponding to
a support-practice factor around 0.5. The benefit peaks on slopes of about 3 to 8 per cent and declines on both
sides — on very gentle land there is little runoff to redirect, and on steep land the ridges are too small to
hold the water that accumulates.

Contouring has a specific and important failure mode that must be designed against. The storage capacity of a
contour ridge is finite, perhaps 10 to 25 millimetres of rainfall depth on a well-formed system. Once exceeded,
water overtops the ridge at its lowest point, and because the entire slope's runoff is concentrated at that one
spot, the resulting breach can gouge a gully in a single storm and cause more damage than no contouring at all.
The remedy is to design in a controlled outlet — a grassed waterway or a diversion — and to accept that contouring
alone is insufficient protection above roughly 8 to 10 per cent slope or where slope lengths exceed about 100 metres.

Practical contouring requires laying out a true contour with an instrument rather than by eye, since the eye is
badly fooled on undulating land. A simple A-frame level of three poles and a plumb bob, calibrated by reversing
it on the same two points, is accurate well within the tolerance required. Where slopes converge and diverge, the true
contour wanders unworkably; the standard compromise is to establish a key contour line, then run parallel rows
from it and absorb the mismatch in short point rows at the awkward end of the field.

Strip cropping multiplies the effect by alternating bands of erosion-prone row crop with bands of dense,
sod-forming cover across the slope. The dense strips act as filters and velocity brakes, trapping sediment
detached above them, so the effective slope length is reduced to the width of a single strip. Recommended strip
widths narrow as slope steepens: roughly 30 metres on a 4 per cent slope, 24 metres at 8 per cent, and 18 metres
or less above 12 per cent. Combined with contouring, strip cropping typically yields a P factor of 0.25 to 0.4,
and it requires no earthmoving and no permanent structures.

Rotation contributes through the C factor rather than P, and its effect is larger than most growers assume.
Alternating a row crop with a small grain and one or more years of perennial forage does three things: it
provides years of near-complete cover, it builds aggregate stability through dense fibrous roots, and it leaves
residual structural benefit that carries into the following row-crop years. A four-year rotation of maize,
soybean, small grain and hay on the same field can carry a weighted C factor a third to a fifth of continuous
row cropping, with no capital cost at all.

sections.heading: Terraces, Diversions and Grassed Waterways
sections.body:
Where slope and rainfall exceed what cover and contouring can hold, the answer is to physically shorten the
slope and to give water a protected route off the field. These are earthworks, and unlike agronomic practices
they must be surveyed, designed to a storm return period, and maintained, or they will fail spectacularly.

A terrace is an earthen embankment or channel built across the slope that intercepts runoff before it accelerates.
Broadbase terraces have gentle side slopes and can be farmed over; they suit gradients up to roughly 8 per cent
and machinery-based agriculture. Narrow-base and steep-backslope terraces occupy less land and suit steeper
ground but take the terrace itself out of production. Bench terraces cut the hillside into a staircase of near-level
platforms with steep risers, at enormous labour cost — the rice terraces of Banaue in the Philippines and the
Andean andenes represent centuries of accumulated construction — but they permit cultivation on slopes of 25 per
cent and beyond. Terraces are further divided by outlet: gradient terraces carry water at a designed slope of
roughly 0.1 to 0.6 per cent to a stable outlet, while level terraces are closed and store water for infiltration,
appropriate only on permeable soils where impoundment will not waterlog or breach. Spacing is set by a formula of
the form vertical interval equals a constant times slope percentage plus another constant; a common working
version gives a vertical interval of about 1.5 to 2.5 metres on cropland, meaning terraces roughly 25 to 40 metres
apart on a 6 per cent slope.

Diversions are individually designed channels placed above the area to be protected — above a gully head, above a
farmstead, above a road cut — to intercept foreign water and lead it away at non-erosive velocity. The governing
number is permissible velocity: about 0.6 to 0.8 metres per second for a bare erodible channel, 1.2 to 1.5 metres
per second for a good grass lining, and 1.8 metres per second or more for dense sod on cohesive soil. Design
capacity is normally the 10-year storm for cropland and the 25-year or 50-year storm where failure would threaten
a building or a road.

Grassed waterways are the shaped, vegetated channels that carry the concentrated flow that terraces and diversions
collect. They are usually broad and shallow — parabolic or trapezoidal, commonly 5 to 20 metres wide and only 30
to 60 centimetres deep — because a wide shallow section spreads flow, keeps depth and therefore velocity low, and
lets machinery cross. Establishment is the hard part: the channel must be shaped, fertilised, seeded to a
vigorous sod species and protected while the sod knits, often for a full season, using straw mulch pinned with
netting or a temporary diversion. A waterway seeded and immediately loaded with runoff will simply become the
gully it was meant to prevent, and the commonest cause of failure is impatience during establishment. Once
established, waterways need annual inspection, occasional reseeding of scoured spots, and a firm rule that
tillage stops at the edge rather than shaving it a little narrower each year.

sections.heading: Windbreaks, Shelterbelts and Surface Roughness
sections.body:
Wind erosion control works on three levers: reduce wind speed at the surface, increase the size and cohesion of
what the wind touches, and shorten the unobstructed distance over which saltation can build. Each lever has a
family of practices.

Reducing wind speed is the job of barriers. A windbreak of trees or shrubs slows wind on its leeward side for a
distance of roughly 10 to 20 times its height H, with the greatest reduction — commonly 50 to 80 per cent — in
the zone from 2H to 8H downwind; there is also a modest protected zone extending 2H to 5H upwind. The critical
design variable is not density but porosity. A solid barrier such as a wall or a dense evergreen hedge creates a
sharp pressure difference, generating strong turbulence and a recirculating eddy that can scour the ground just
behind it. A permeable barrier of roughly 40 to 50 per cent optical porosity lets enough air bleed through to
suppress that eddy and produces the longest and smoothest protected zone. Multi-row belts combining a shrub row,
a deciduous row and a conifer row achieve this reliably; a single row of widely spaced trees does not. Orientation
should be perpendicular to the prevailing erosive wind, which in many regions is not the prevailing annual wind
but the seasonal wind that coincides with bare soil, and spacing between parallel belts is normally set at 10 to
15 H.

Increasing what the wind touches means roughness and cohesion at the surface. Standing stubble is dramatically
more effective than flattened residue of the same mass, because vertical stalks extract momentum through their
whole height; stubble 25 to 30 centimetres tall at moderate density can suppress erosion almost completely.
Emergency tillage exploits the same principle in reverse: running a chisel or lister across the wind on a
threatened field brings up clods 25 to 75 millimetres across, which are too heavy to move and which shelter the
fines between them. It is a crude, one-off measure that damages structure and should be reserved for an
imminent event on a field that would otherwise blow, but it works within hours. Ridging perpendicular to the wind
adds the same roughness more durably.

Shortening the fetch is the third lever and is often the cheapest. Because saltation needs 50 to 100 metres of
bare surface to reach full intensity, strips of standing crop, cover crop, or even unharvested rows placed at
intervals across the wind repeatedly reset the chain reaction to zero. Field strip cropping in alternating bands
perpendicular to the erosive wind is the classic Great Plains implementation and requires no permanent
plantings.

Finally, moisture and crusting matter enormously and are the reason wind erosion is a spring and autumn problem.
Soil above roughly 4 to 6 per cent gravimetric water content in the surface centimetre resists movement almost
entirely. Irrigating a vulnerable field ahead of a forecast wind event is a legitimate emergency measure where
water is available, and preserving a natural rain crust by not tilling before a windy period costs nothing.

sections.heading: Building the Soil So It Resists: Organic Matter, Aggregates and Roots
sections.body:
Structural practices manage water that is already running off. The deeper cure is to make the soil absorb the
rain in the first place, and that capacity is overwhelmingly a function of aggregate stability, which is in turn
a function of organic matter and biological activity. A degraded silt loam at 1.5 per cent organic matter may
accept 10 millimetres of rain per hour before sealing; the same soil rebuilt to 4 per cent organic matter with
continuous living roots may accept 50 to 100 millimetres per hour. Since erosion requires runoff, and runoff
requires rainfall to exceed infiltration, a soil that swallows an intense storm simply does not erode regardless
of its slope.

The mechanism runs through several layers. Organic matter supplies the polysaccharide gums and humic compounds
that cement particles into water-stable aggregates. Fungal hyphae, particularly of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi,
physically bind aggregates together with threads that can extend tens of centimetres from a root; a hectare of
healthy grassland soil may contain thousands of kilometres of hyphae. Fine roots enmesh soil directly and, on
dying, leave channels and a legacy of exudates. Earthworms are structural engineers in their own right: anecic
species such as the common nightcrawler drive permanent vertical burrows several millimetres wide and up to two
metres deep that conduct water into the subsoil far faster than the matrix around them, and their casts are
notably more stable than bulk soil. A population of 200 earthworms per square metre can produce burrows conducting
several hundred millimetres of water per hour.

Practices that build this system are consistent across climates and scales. Keep a living root in the ground as
many days of the year as possible, because roots feed the biology continuously while dead residue feeds it only
in pulses; this is the strongest single argument for cover crops beyond their surface protection. Add carbon —
compost, manure, straw, wood chip — accepting that raising organic matter by one percentage point in the top 15
centimetres requires on the order of 20 to 30 tonnes of stable carbon-rich material per hectare and several years,
because most added carbon is respired away. Minimise tillage, which shears hyphal networks, breaks worm burrows
and exposes protected organic matter to rapid oxidation. Diversify the plant community, since different root
architectures build structure at different depths. Manage calcium and sodium, since flocculated clay aggregates
and dispersed clay does not.

Two honest caveats belong here. First, the timescales are years to decades, not seasons; a soil degraded over a
century does not rebuild in three years, and claims of rapid transformation should be checked against measured
aggregate stability rather than accepted. Second, high organic matter does not confer immunity. An intense
storm falling on a saturated soil will run off no matter how good its structure, because infiltration cannot
proceed into pores already full. Structure buys enormous resilience; it does not repeal hydrology.

sections.heading: Stopping an Active Gully: A Working Procedure
sections.body:
An advancing gully is the most urgent form of erosion because it destroys land permanently, drains adjacent soil,
and grows faster each year as its catchment enlarges. The governing insight is that a gully is powered by water
arriving at its head from upslope. Filling it without addressing that water simply provides fresh material to be
removed. Work from the top of the catchment down, never from the gully up, and treat structures as a way of
buying time while vegetation establishes rather than as the permanent solution. For anything deeper than about
1.5 metres, or where failure would threaten a road, building or public safety, get engineered design and consent
before excavating — an undersized structure concentrates flow and can make matters far worse.
steps: Map the contributing catchment first: walk upslope from the gully head after rain and mark every path by which water arrives, including road ditches, roof and yard drainage, compacted tracks and field furrows. Estimate the area in hectares, because the whole design depends on it.

Cut the water off at source wherever possible. Divert road and yard runoff to a stable vegetated outlet, break up compacted tracks, and re-route field furrows onto the contour. Reducing inflow by half is worth more than any structure you can build in the channel.

Build a diversion or terrace across the slope above the gully head, sized for at least the 10-year storm, with a designed grass outlet leading away from the gully. Keep channel velocity below about 1.2 metres per second on grass.
Shape the head itself. Batter the vertical headcut back to a stable slope no steeper than about 2 horizontal to 1 vertical, so it can hold vegetation instead of undermining and collapsing.

Install grade-control structures in the channel where residual flow remains. Loose rock check dams 30 to 60 centimetres high, keyed at least 30 centimetres into both banks and the bed, with a lowered central notch so water overtops in the middle and not around the ends, and a rock apron below to absorb the plunge.
Space the checks so the crest of each sits level with the toe of the one above, which flattens the effective grade. On a 5 per cent bed with 45-centimetre dams, that is roughly one every 9 metres.
Reshape the banks to a mowable slope, spread any stockpiled topsoil, and seed a vigorous sod mixture at a heavy rate with a nurse crop for quick cover.
Mulch immediately with straw at about 4 tonnes per hectare, anchored by crimping or netting, or lay erosion-control matting on the steepest faces. Bare seeded soil will wash before it germinates.
Exclude livestock and machinery completely for at least two full growing seasons, then inspect after every major storm, repairing scour and reseeding thin patches before the next event enlarges them.

sections.heading: Garden, Smallholding and Building-Site Practice
sections.body:
The same physics governs a quarter-hectare vegetable plot, a new house lot and a thousand-hectare farm, but the
scale changes which tools are practical. On small ground, labour is available and machinery is not, so
protection tends to be materials-based rather than earthwork-based, and results come quickly because a small area
can be fully covered.

The core moves are unchanged. Never leave bed surfaces bare between crops; sow a quick cover such as buckwheat,
field peas, oats or mustard even for a six-week gap. Mulch permanently on paths and around perennials, since
paths carry most of the concentrated flow in a garden and are usually the first place a rill appears. Run beds
across the slope rather than down it, and edge them so each becomes a small level terrace. Where the ground
exceeds about 15 per cent, build simple bench terraces with timber, stone or woven-brush risers, working
progressively from the bottom of the slope upward so that each new bench is supported by the one below.

Newly disturbed construction ground is the most erodible surface most people ever encounter, often losing 20 to
200 tonnes per hectare per year — one to two orders of magnitude more than farmland — because it is bare,
compacted and steep. The professional rule is to strip and stockpile topsoil separately, to expose the smallest
area for the shortest time, to protect stockpiles with seed or cover, and to install perimeter controls before
earthmoving begins rather than after the first storm. Silt fences trap coarse sediment but do almost nothing for
clay, so they are a supplement to surface cover, never a substitute.
ingredients: Straw or hay mulch, weed-free, applied 5 to 8 centimetres deep; roughly one small square bale per 10 to 15 square metres. Source from a local grower and ask about herbicide history, since some broadleaf herbicides persist in hay and damage vegetables.
Wood chip from a tree surgeon, usually free by the load, for paths and around perennials but not dug into vegetable beds where it can tie up nitrogen.

Cover crop seed: buckwheat for fast summer cover, oats or rye for winter, field peas or vetch to add nitrogen, mustard for a quick catch crop. Farm supply merchants sell these far cheaper by the kilogram than garden centres by the packet.
Erosion-control matting of jute, coir or straw for slopes steeper than about 3 to 1, pinned with U-shaped steel staples every 60 to 90 centimetres.
Compost or well-rotted manure to build aggregate stability, at 25 to 50 millimetres spread annually.
Gravel, 20 to 40 millimetre grade, for permanent paths, gateways and downpipe outfalls where flow concentrates.
An A-frame level or a line level and string to lay out true contours before building beds or terraces.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Honest Limits and What to Do When It Goes Wrong
sections.body:
Conservation systems fail in a small number of recognisable ways, and knowing them is more useful than knowing
another practice. The most common failure is concentration: a well-protected field with one unprotected flow
path loses far more than a uniformly mediocre one, because runoff finds the weakness and the fifth-power
relationship between velocity and transport does the rest. Wheel tracks, headlands, gateways, the ends of
terraces, the shaved edge of a waterway and the outfall of a roof downpipe are the usual offenders. Walking a
site during heavy rain, unpleasant as it is, reveals more in twenty minutes than a season of dry inspection.

The second failure is undersizing. Structures designed for a 10-year storm will, by definition, be overtopped
roughly once a decade, and a breached terrace can gouge a gully worse than the erosion it prevented. Where the
consequence of failure is severe, design for a longer return period and provide a deliberate, armoured overflow
point so that when the structure is exceeded it fails in a place and manner you have chosen.

The third is the establishment gap. Newly seeded waterways, reshaped banks and freshly terraced ground are at
their most vulnerable precisely when they are newest. The interval between construction and full sod cover, often
a whole season, must be bridged with mulch, matting or temporary diversion, and construction should be timed so
that gap does not coincide with the region's most erosive months.

The fourth is maintenance drift. Terraces silt up, waterways are narrowed a metre a year by tillage, windbreaks
develop gaps at the base as lower branches die, check dams fill and are overtopped at the ends. All of these
degrade slowly and invisibly until a large storm exposes them. An annual walk with a written checklist is the
cheapest insurance in the whole discipline.

Several honest limits deserve stating plainly. No practice prevents erosion in a genuinely extreme event; a
200-millimetre rainfall on saturated ground will move soil off well-managed land. Prediction models carry large
uncertainty on individual fields and cannot model gullies, tillage erosion or bank failure. Some techniques trade
against other goals: terraces consume land and capital, no-till may increase dissolved phosphorus loss and
herbicide dependence, and heavy mulch can harbour slugs and delay soil warming. Regenerating a soil eroded to
subsoil may take decades and, on thin soils over rock, may be effectively irreversible.

When damage occurs, the sequence is consistent. Stabilise the active feature first, before the next storm — mulch,
matting, a temporary diversion, straw bales staked across a rill. Then find and fix the water source rather than
the symptom. Then rebuild the surface with cover and roots. Then, and only then, consider whether a permanent
structure is genuinely needed, because a great many gullies that were about to be engineered turned out to have
been caused by a single misdirected culvert.
